entries.title: A Fix for Softmax and Cross-Entropy
summary: The paper rewrites softmax and cross-entropy computations to preserve small gradients that ordinary floating-point formulations can erase or corrupt.

Correcting high-confidence rounding and near-identical teacher–student cancellation prevents training spikes and distillation drift in controlled small-model experiments, providing a diagnostic and implementation fix for sensitive optimization regimes.

evidence.rationale: Pinned v1 full ten-page PDF and HTML, Sections 1–8, Equations 1–11, Table 1, all experimental figures and inline JAX implementations inspected. Standard overflow-safe softmax can still round the confident target probability to one while leaving positive non-target gradients, breaking the exact zero-sum gradient identity; the paper reformulates the target/non-target computation using a stable margin and softplus. A separate logits-aware distillation construction uses log1p/expm1 and a projected custom gradient to preserve small teacher–student differences instead of subtracting independently rounded probabilities. This second construction requires teacher logits, not only already-rounded target probabilities. The hard-target precision cliffs are approximately margin 5.5 in bfloat16, 16.6 in float32 and 36.7 in float64; casting up delays the cliff. Controlled grokking experiments include one-layer Transformers and two-layer MLPs on modular arithmetic. The principal modular-addition experiment uses a one-layer width-64 Transformer, modulus 31, a 50% training split and 10,000 full-batch AdamW epochs. Table 1 sweeps three precisions and three Adam epsilon values over five seeds; at float32 and epsilon 1e-8, the fixed formulation reports 100.0% mean test accuracy versus 94.3% for standard cross-entropy. The distillation diagnostic begins with a student identical to an already-correct modular-arithmetic teacher, uses temperature 4, 2,000 Adam steps and three seeds, and demonstrates drift from numerical cancellation rather than useful learning from a stronger teacher. Prior work already identified collapse/slingshot behavior and proposed mitigations; the contribution is the direct stable formulation and joint numerical/optimization analysis, not the first observation of all such failures. Original receipt October 22 17:54:56 UTC retained. The original Friday October 23 cs.LG new-submission batch and official Eastern-time schedule imply paper announcement October 23 00:00 UTC. No earlier release of this complete paper/formulation was found in the bounded exact-title/author-artifact search; negative search is not proof of absence. The inspected primary paper includes implementations, but no separate author code/project release was verified.
evidence.limitations: Evidence is controlled small-model arithmetic/grokking and near-identical-network distillation, not a demonstrated improvement in ordinary large-scale LLM training or downstream language capability. The authors explicitly note that the extreme confidence and near-zero teacher–student gaps may be uncommon in standard large-scale regimes. Results across precisions and optimizer epsilon settings do not establish a universal accuracy gain or an optimizer-independent training guarantee. The distillation fix needs logits and custom gradient handling, so it is not automatically a drop-in change for every fused kernel or probability-only interface. No LLM-scale throughput/latency benchmark or independent reproduction was verified.

entries.title: BeNice! Closing Looping's Inference-Memory Gap via KV-Sharing
summary: BeNice adds an auxiliary fine-tuning objective that makes a looped language model’s early pass compatible with the final pass’s cached keys and values, enabling the recurrences to share one history cache.

On the tested Parcae models, it largely preserves the quality of ordinary fine-tuning while removing the recurrence-dependent cache duplication, offering a way to increase inference depth without proportional growth in cache memory.

evidence.rationale: Pinned v1 PDF (37 pages), HTML main methods/results and relevant evaluation, convergence, LoRA and training appendices inspected. The primary novelty is supervised adaptation, hence category1.5 rather than the application category3.4. Stochastic-depth pretraining uses per-sequence Poisson recurrence depth; the new objective combines ordinary final-recurrence cross-entropy with an auxiliary hybrid predictor using first-recurrence queries/residuals and final-recurrence KV. This avoids training through complete sequential shared-cache rollouts. The diagnosis localizes failures in released770M/1.3B Parcae models to a low-rank first-layer/first-recurrence residual shift; stochastic-depth convergence alone does not ensure the same shared/unshared fixed point. Full fine-tuning uses140M tokens; a rank8 first-layer key/value LoRA variant uses65M tokens and41K/49K trainable parameters. Table5 compares independently tuned standard fine-tuning and BeNice over three seeds: released770M shared validation perplexity21.61→11.86 while unshared remains11.86 versus11.85; the1.3B shared result18.52→10.78 accompanies unshared10.79 for both. Newly pretrained140M–1.3B models and22-task Core/46-task Core-Extended suites support the mechanism; the new370M shared Core score rises15.16→23.51. Section5.3 separately reports1.3B Parcae global HBM63.82→21.60GB at batch64/context2048 (weights, cache, graphs and buffers included), and proxy looped-model Mooncake/AIPerf workload experiments: at2requests/s cache hits rise8.1percentage points, throughput23.6%, and p90 time to first token139.2→23.2seconds. These serving proxies are distinct from the quality-tested BeNice models. Receipt is2026-10-22T17:49:44Z; the original FridayOct23 cs.LG batch plus official Thursday20:00US/Eastern posting schedule imply announcement2026-10-23T00:00Z, within this daily window. Earlier looped KV sharing and Parcae checkpoints are background, not claimed as new. No earlier BeNice release or author implementation/project destination was verified in the inspected primary text and exact-title search.
evidence.limitations: The empirical adaptation results concern140M–1.3B Parcae-family models, finite task suites and mostly2048-token training contexts; they do not establish quality preservation for arbitrary looped architectures, frontier models or all context lengths. The convergence theorem assumes a contractive recurrent block and Lipschitz KV projections; stochastic-depth training is not proven to make every model contractive. First-layer localization/mean patching is not universal across all newly trained models, and Kimi delta-attention variants already share state well without extra adaptation. Prelude/coda caches remain, so total KV is not reduced by exactly1/T, and recurrences still consume computation. Low-precision composition is a quality study, not an independently measured FP4 kernel speedup. The serving section explicitly simulates the memory-constrained regime with proxies constructed by looping existing weights such as GLM4.7-FP8; their downstream quality is not shown to match BeNice-trained models, and serving GPU type/count is not specified in the inspected setup. Low-load workloads show little latency/throughput gain. No general production or quality-preserving frontier serving speedup, public BeNice code release, or independent reproduction is claimed.

entries.title: When to Follow the Teacher: Advantage-Based On-Policy Distillation
summary: AOPD weights teacher guidance by whether the suggested action helps the current student succeed, rather than treating every teacher-preferred token as beneficial.

An estimator built from rewarded student rollouts improves several tested math and coding distillation results without extra teacher rollouts or a learned value model, although it requires outcome rewards and does not win every benchmark.

evidence.rationale: Pinned v1 full 22-page PDF and HTML, method Section 3, experiments Section 4 and Tables 1–4, policy-space analysis Section 5 and relevant proof, setup, sampling, group-size, clipping and implementation appendices inspected. The objective favors teacher actions with positive advantage under student continuations. A change-of-measure estimator combines a sampled teacher/student probability ratio and a dense teacher expectation with a leave-one-out terminal-reward baseline from the same response group. It does not require explicit teacher-action continuation rollouts. Ratio clipping at c=4 caps the teacher measure in both terms without renormalizing it, estimating a modified clipped objective rather than preserving exact unbiasedness for the original unclipped objective. Main comparisons use LoRA rank 64, batch size 32 and non-thinking Qwen models. External math distills Qwen3-4B-Instruct into Qwen3-1.7B for 450 updates; external coding uses a Qwen3-8B teacher and 350 updates. Table 1 reports AIME24 pass@1 of 35.0% versus 32.6% for the strongest listed alternative on that metric, OPD with reverse KL, and AMC 65.1% versus 61.8%. This is not uniform dominance: HMMT is 15.8% versus 16.0% for forward-KL OPD, and other coding metrics also favor alternatives. Self-distillation conditions the same base student on a reference solution; Qwen3-8B reaches AIME24 52.1% versus 41.7% for OPSD in Table 2. Tables 3–4 include mixed domain/model outcomes, including a Qwen3-4B biology regression. Paper reward-improvement results concern exact, sufficiently small KL-proximal policy-space updates under their assumptions, not arbitrary finite-sample neural SGD. The verified author repository and pinned first substantive/current READMEs disclose a residual correction beyond the paper clipped objective and an optional forward-KL term only for all-zero-reward groups; external math uses mu=0.08. Those release additions and paper/source setting differences must not be erased in a reproduction. Original arXiv receipt October 22 17:05:21 UTC retained; original paper announcement is in the October 23 batch. Repository creation October 13 does not establish an earlier method release: the inspected complete 154-commit history starts with a LICENSE-only October 21 23:21:44 UTC commit, followed by substantive README/code from October 21 23:27:24 onward, within the 72-hour lookback. Commit dates do not prove the precise moment a repository became public. This is conservatively newly-discovered catch-up first inspected today, without claiming an indexing delay or resetting the method age to its paper announcement.
evidence.limitations: AOPD requires terminal outcome rewards and teacher probabilities on student prefixes; unlike pure distillation it is not reward-free. No extra reward evaluations means reuse of already-rewarded RL rollouts, not zero scoring cost versus OPD. Main comparisons have method-specific sampling/tuning and different response-group sizes for some RL baselines, so equal update counts do not establish matched total compute or rollout budgets. No broad independent-training-seed uncertainty study is reported for the main benchmark comparisons. Results vary by task, model and metric, with explicit regressions; no general superiority to every teacher/distillation/RL baseline is established. Clipping modifies the objective, and the exact proximal theoretical guarantee does not directly cover the released residual correction or practical LoRA updates. Repository READMEs document differences between paper-default launchers and retained experiment-source settings. No training code was executed and no independent reproduction was performed.

entries.title: RoleFlow: Self-Evolving Multi-Role Agentic Collaboration via Structural Adaptation
summary: RoleFlow learns to revise a team of specialist agents one structural edit at a time, using paired training executions with and without each edit to assign credit to the change.

Its trained router improves multi-hop question answering with a frozen executor and transfers to two unseen QA benchmarks, offering a concrete approach to learning adaptive collaboration rather than choosing a fixed workflow.

evidence.rationale: Sections 3–4, Tables 1–3 and Appendices A–C specify a Qwen2.5-7B router, frozen gpt-4o-mini executor, validator feedback, on-demand role synthesis and ADD/PRUNE/SWAP/REROUTE edits. SECPO executes edited and unchanged chains at the same state during training, adds their reward difference only to edit tokens on top of GRPO credit, and retains an edit above a 0.005 advantage threshold; rejected edits still train the router. With three training runs, Table 2 reports HotpotQA/2Wiki/MuSiQue F1 of 55.6/43.5/42.1 versus 53.5/41.0/39.5 for GRPO. The latter two use the HotpotQA-trained router without retraining. QA uses one chain per question; each chain allows three adaptation cycles after its initial execution. MATH uses 20 chains and coding 10 chains with final selection, so those reported results are not single-sample inference. Appendix A.3/B states WebShop uses the MBPP-trained router, overriding the looser main-text wording. Receipt 2026-10-21T20:37:32Z is preserved; original cs.AI October 23 new-submission listing plus the official schedule supports inferred 2026-10-23T00:00Z availability. No earlier matching author artifact was established in bounded checks.
evidence.limitations: Results depend on task-specific validation and the tested router/executor. Counterfactual training increases realized executions per QA task from 9.1 to 13.5; unequal baseline training and inference budgets limit broad ranking claims. Coding/math use multiple samples, and the WebShop validator can replace invalid or purchase-blocking actions. SECPO slightly trails GRPO on MBPP and ties it on HumanEval. Inference starts from seed roles rather than the training-grown library. No matching author code repository was verified; this is a primary-paper assessment, not an independent reproduction.

entries.title: SWE-VERIFIER: Selective Verification for Cost-Efficient Coding Agents
summary: SWE-VERIFIER trains a small model to inspect proposed coding-agent actions and requests alternative candidates only when the original action receives a low score.

On 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks it raises MiniMax-M2.7 resolution from 75.47% to 77.20% while verifying 3.43% of steps, suggesting that selective checking can control policy-API spending; the reported 1.09× cost excludes local verifier inference.

evidence.rationale: Sections 2–4, Tables 1–3 and Appendices A–D describe Qwen3.5-4B verification, action-conditioned rubric generation followed by scoring, threshold gating and reranking before executing an action. Training uses 500 successful SWE-Smith trajectories, sampled alternative actions and immediate tool feedback, with a stronger teacher labeling 30,000 actions across 6,000 states; the deployed student sees task/history/proposed action, not that action’s future execution result. On all 500 SWE-bench Verified tasks in mini-swe-agent, Table 1 reports MiniMax-M2.7 75.47±1.40 to 77.20±0.87 and DeepSeek-V4-Flash-correct-high 72.60±0.53 to 74.27±1.01. Their verified-step shares are 3.43%/3.59% and policy-API cost factors 1.09×/1.13×, under an explicit zero-cost assumption for local verifier inference. The 202-task threshold-selection subset overlaps the full 500-task evaluation. Receipt 2026-10-21T18:02:33Z is preserved; the original cs.LG October 23 new-submission listing, not just a cs.AI cross-list, and the official schedule support inferred 2026-10-23T00:00Z availability.
evidence.limitations: API cost accounting treats the local 4B verifier as free and does not establish total serving cost, latency, energy or training savings. Threshold selection overlaps evaluated tasks, and the main Table 1 does not fully define the reported variation or repetition count, so no significance claim is made. Labels are derived from successful trajectories and teacher rubrics; sampled-action distribution shift remains relevant. The paper-linked GitHub repository and API/README/tree/history endpoints returned 404 during this run, so no released-code link is published and reproducibility could not be checked.

entries.title: Memory-Aware Reward Modeling: Learning Human Preferences for LLM Memory Use
summary: This study asks whether personal memories actually make an assistant’s answers more useful to the person who supplied them, combining user judgments with an interpretable rubric-based preference model.

On 291 strong-preference pairs, participant-held-out evaluation reaches 72.8% prediction accuracy versus a 55.0% majority baseline, giving developers a way to evaluate appropriate memory use beyond factual recall.

evidence.rationale: Sections 3–6 and Appendices A–F report 821 quality-filtered judgments from 87 participants, comparing responses generated with and without nine retrieved personal-memory entries. Candidate pairs were screened for substantial memory-grounded differences before annotation. Under ordinary prompting, memory/no-memory/tie preferences are 38.7%/41.9%/19.4%; direction differs by response generator. The learned model uses rubric features and L2 logistic regression on the 291 clear “much better” pairs. Rubric induction, standardization and nested regularization selection use training participants only; five participant-separated folds are repeated across ten shuffles, with predictions averaged before accuracy. Table 3 reports 72.8% overall accuracy against a 55.0% majority baseline; response-only features achieve 67.0%. Receipt 2026-10-22T13:43:33Z is preserved; original cs.CL October 23 new-submission listing plus the official schedule supports inferred 2026-10-23T00:00Z availability. No earlier matching author release was established.
evidence.limitations: This is a small, screened offline preference study, not representative evidence for all assistant queries or a trained memory-management policy. Only 291 strong-preference pairs enter the learned-model evaluation; aggregate prompting differences are descriptive and vary by generator. Length and heading features are influential, so gains cannot be attributed solely to memory-specific judgment. It does not measure longitudinal agent behavior or downstream RL improvements. Some baseline-label wording and collection-prompt counts differ between main text and appendices; claims here use the stable table values and avoid the disputed labels/counts. No public author code or dataset artifact was verified.

entries.title: LLMs are making formal software verification feasible at a much larger scale
summary: Anthropic and Theorem use Claude to turn existing fuzz-test entry points into specifications for compiled programs, then generate proofs that Rocq checks against modeled execution semantics.
This makes proof-producing coding agents a concrete software-hardening workflow, while the guarantees remain conditional on the particular binaries, specifications and trusted models.

evidence.rationale: The complete blog and six-page appendix describe the workflow and report proofs for 239 entry points across 123 libraries, with an input bound of 64 MiB; the inspected public release contains proofs for 60 entry points in 25 libraries. The release README and origin documentation specify exact binaries, statement checking and allowed assumptions. This is a new dated research disclosure with inspectable proof artifacts; no proof checker was executed here.
evidence.limitations: The public statements concern fixed-budget, static RISC-V/Linux binaries and reachable harness behavior, rather than whole-library correctness or deployed x86/ARM systems. The released agreement proofs do not establish termination. Patches regenerate specifications, creating a potential shortcut that the authors report auditing; semantics, theorem statements, checker and tooling remain trusted. Reported research scale exceeds the released subset.

entries.title: Gandalf: Flash Shall Not Die! Increasing Flash Storage Lifetime for KV Cache Offloading in LLM Serving
summary: Gandalf manages offloaded attention caches across host memory and solid-state drives, using attention type, expected reuse and write wear to decide which states to retain, move or recompute.

Its trace-based evaluation shows how avoiding low-value writes can extend projected drive endurance, giving serving-system designers an explicit way to trade cache misses against storage wear rather than optimizing hit rate alone.

evidence.rationale: Full14-page pinned v1 PDF and HTML methods/results inspected. The central contribution is a storage admission/placement policy, category3.7. Full-attention prefixes can be reused across successive turns, whereas recurrent/linear states are often reused only at the next turn and then superseded. Each admitted state first enters DRAM; under pressure Gandalf compares a leaf-drop cost with moving a root-side candidate to SSD, counting estimated next-reuse recomputation benefit, object size, idle age, SSD purchase price per rated write byte and the loss from replacing an SSD victim. An optional target-lifetime multiplier prices writes more aggressively when the write budget is overspent. Lazy heaps over prefix-tree leaf/frontier candidates reduce scoring work. The online rule approximates an offline objective; it is not a proved optimal replacement algorithm. Main evaluation uses three traces (Qwen Bailian TraceA, ClaudeCode WEKA SemiAnalysis, and a400K-request/100-turn AIPerf workload), a Kimi-K3 hybrid configuration with72% linear-attention layers,100GB host DRAM and1TB/4TB SSD capacities, and six policies adapted to the same two-tier capacity. At the minimum-miss setting in Section5.2, ClaudeCode has Gandalf miss ratio0.052 versus0.045 for Marconi/0.047 for LRU, while the latter write3.3× more SSD bytes; projected rated-endurance lifetime follows the write-volume reduction. The paper separately models a practical tradeoff at alpha1:17.0 versus4.0 months projected life at0.78 versus0.66seconds modeled cache-load latency, assuming10GB/s SSD,50GB/s host-to-GPU transfer and60Ktokens/s recomputation. This is not measured end-to-end GPU latency. Receipt is2026-10-22T06:10:08Z; the original FridayOct23 cs.LG batch and official Thursday20:00US/Eastern schedule imply announcement2026-10-23T00:00Z. Exact-title screening did not establish an earlier public Gandalf method. No author implementation/project release destination was verified; background LMCache/vLLM links are not presented as Gandalf source code.
evidence.limitations: Principal comparative results are trace-based simulation, with small-scale FEMU emulator calibration and an author-stated LMCache/vLLM integration; the paper does not provide measured physical drive wear-out or deployment throughput demonstrating the policy. Lifetime means time to consume rated TBW under indefinitely repeated traces, a1DWPD/five-year rating and write-amplification factor1. SSD garbage collection, internal wear leveling, changing production mixes and physical failure uncertainty are not modeled, so lifetime is a projection and can be optimistic. The headline7.3× average does not describe every matched miss-rate setting; alpha can incur large miss penalties (TraceA0.818 versus LRU0.697 at alpha1), and the paper’s separate analyses use different settings. Cache-load latency assumes transfer/recomputation overlap and fixed rates; it is not whole-request TTFT or a hardware benchmark. Next-turn reuse/type assumptions fit append-only hybrid workloads, not arbitrary cache branching or all architectures. Heap candidate pruning is validated on two traces, not universally lossless. No independent reproduction or verified public Gandalf code release; extension to high-bandwidth flash is future work.

entries.title: Loopholing All the Way: Language Modeling with pure Self-Conditioning
summary: LAW repeatedly refines continuous expected token embeddings and samples discrete tokens only at the end, making self-conditioning the complete generative state rather than an auxiliary hint.
Matched-training-compute experiments improve constraint solving and small-scale mathematical reasoning, suggesting an alternative to interleaving discrete token resampling with denoising.
The evidence does not yet establish frontier-scale quality or wall-clock speedups.

evidence.rationale: Pinned v1 Sections 3–5 and relevant task, compute, training and generation appendices inspected. LAW initializes token embeddings from uniformly sampled tokens, feeds a noncausal denoiser only the continuous self-conditioning state, and updates that state with the probability-weighted expected token embedding. Prompt positions remain fixed clean embeddings, and a categorical token projection is deferred to the end. Training still uses a discrete-diffusion-corrupted initialization and task-specific cross-entropy or negative-ELBO objectives; pure self-conditioning describes sampling, not absence of a diffusion-derived training objective. Default training uses two passes with probability 0.9, stop-gradient between passes and loss only on the final pass, with randomized self-conditioning temperature; OpenWebText also uses a learned mode embedding. Estimated training FLOPs count a backward pass as twice a forward pass, so these settings cost 3.9 forward-pass equivalents per update versus 3 for the comparison, and LAW uses about 77% as many steps. Academic 8-layer and 12-layer DiT experiments cover Sudoku, mazes, TinyGSM-to-GSM8K and OpenWebText. The reported hard Sudoku score is 96.5% versus 91.0% for the retrained LDDM-U comparison at 180 function evaluations. The matched-FLOP 12-layer TinyGSM study reports 42.2% GSM8K accuracy versus 34.5% for LDDM-U at temperature 1 and 1,024 function evaluations. The Maze metric accepts any valid shortest path, rather than reference-path exact match. OpenWebText evidence uses external-model generative perplexity alongside unigram entropy, with a quality/diversity tradeoff as iterations increase; it is not a measured wall-clock speed comparison. The original October 21 receipt (17:25:08 UTC) is retained. The original October 22 new-submission batch and official Eastern-time schedule imply October 22 00:00 UTC availability; no earlier primary artifact was verified in the bounded search. The paper-announced author code URL and GitHub API both return 404, so no available-code link is claimed.
evidence.limitations: The tested models and contexts are small academic setups, with task-specific objectives and tuned sampling settings; no frontier-scale language or chat capability result is established. Matched estimated training FLOPs do not mean matched wall-clock time, and numbers of function evaluations are not end-to-end latency. The paper mixes retrained comparisons and prior reported puzzle results, so the evidence should not be generalized into universal benchmark leadership. Main reported results do not provide a broad multi-training-seed uncertainty study. OpenWebText external-model perplexity and unigram entropy are incomplete quality/diversity proxies. Training still uses diffusion corruption and, for some tasks, a diffusion-derived bound. The announced author repository was unavailable (404), limiting artifact verification. No independent reproduction.

entries.title: Data Schedules and Learning Rate Schedules Should Be Designed Together
summary: Controlled experiments show that a data-mixture schedule can help or hurt mid-training depending on when the learning rate decays, even when total compute and target-data tokens are fixed.

Dense and mixture-of-experts experiments favor keeping the rate high after target data first appears and using a short final cooldown to lower target-domain validation loss, giving recipe designers a reason to tune the two schedules together.

evidence.rationale: Pinned v1 Sections 2–4 and relevant setup, repeat-run, data-schedule and cooldown appendices inspected. The study holds continuation compute and mid-training token budget fixed while varying the target-data fraction over time and the learning-rate schedule, across over 250 runs with a 630M dense model and a 2.99B-total-parameter MoE model (454M active non-embedding parameters plus embeddings). The dense model continues for 20.97152B tokens after 200B DCLM pretraining; the MoE main study uses 4B or 10B continuation tokens after 40B pretraining. FineMath is the principal target corpus, with code-data checks as well. Two-stage jumps and zero-then-linear ramps interact differently with constant learning rates and full- or matching-window decay: earlier mixing can help under full decay but lose its advantage under a constant rate. Across 19 tested cooldown sweeps, the best tested decay spans 10–40% of the mid-training window, rather than necessarily beginning when target data first appears. A ramp can have twice the mid-training window at the same target-token budget, so fractional cooldowns must also be compared in absolute steps. For example, the dense 25%-budget two-stage configuration reaches target validation cross-entropy 1.4275 with a 40% cooldown versus 1.4717 with constant learning rate and 1.4475 with decay over the matching mid-training range. These are configured-tokenizer loss units, not downstream accuracy. Selected configurations are repeated with three data-stream/order replicates sharing the same pretrained checkpoint; most sweeps have one run. Fresh optimizer state, no continuation warmup, and the within-family optimizer settings are held fixed. The original October 21 receipt (07:42:20 UTC) is retained. The paper appears in the original October 22 new-submission batch; October 22 00:00 UTC availability is inferred from that dated batch and the official Eastern-time announcement schedule. No earlier primary release was found in the bounded title/artifact search, which does not prove absence of one. The paper cites prior curriculum and schedule studies; the contribution is its controlled budget comparisons and recipe evidence, not the first observation that data and optimization interact.
evidence.limitations: Evidence concerns target-domain validation loss at these model/data scales, not established downstream capability gains or a universal optimum. Pretraining loss can trade off against target loss. Only a few configurations have data-order repeats, and they share one pretrained checkpoint; close loss differences are not automatically statistically significant. The dense and MoE families have different tokenizers and optimizer details, so absolute losses are not directly comparable across families. The noisy-quadratic/SGD analysis explains the interaction under assumptions rather than proving the best schedule for Transformers. The 10–40% cooldown range is the best among tested choices, not a universal rule. No author implementation/project release was verified from the inspected primary source, and no independent reproduction was performed.

entries.title: EPIC: Rethinking Trust Regions for Autoregressive LLM Policies via Exact-KL Prefix Importance-Ratio Clipping
summary: EPIC limits policy drift over generated prefixes instead of clipping each token independently or treating a whole response as one unit.

Its probability-calibrated prefix objective improves benchmark-selected mathematical reasoning in the tested off-policy mixture-of-experts setup without storing expert-routing decisions, offering an alternative to routing replay.

evidence.rationale: Pinned v1 Section 3 (prefix change of measure, exact-KL coordinates and practical objective), the main experiments and relevant implementation/ablation appendices inspected, together with the author repository, pinned initial README and current IMPLEMENTATION.md. EPIC starts from cumulative prefix importance ratios and the reverse-KL coordinate r - 1 - log(r); practical clipping budgets depend on prefix length and geometric mean behavior probability. It uses a geometric-mean ratio, detached prefix weights with current-token-only gradients, sign-aware clipping and implementation log-weight caps. The exact identity does not make the resulting optimization surrogate a hard distribution-level KL constraint. Main experiments train Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base on 17,917 processed DAPO-Math entries with 32 A100 GPUs, 300 steps, 64 prompts times 8 responses per rollout, eight minibatches and one PPO epoch, comparing six methods over three independent training runs. Evaluation uses 130 distinct questions across AIME 2024/2025, AMC 2023 and HMMT February 2025, with eight responses per question. Mean@8 averages binary correctness over the samples; it is not pass@8. Table 1 reports a four-benchmark average of 39.34% for EPIC versus 35.45% for DAPO, the strongest comparison average, and 32.84% for GSPO. Each run selects its best checkpoint using this same four-benchmark average, so these are benchmark-selected results. The separate routing-replay study reports 77.5% and 93.0% lower driver-process CPU resident memory than its R2 and R3 implementations, respectively; these are not GPU-memory or whole-cluster reductions. The original paper receipt is October 21 16:37:09 UTC and its original new-submission announcement is October 22. An inspected initial implementation commit, authored and committed October 20 07:41:35 UTC, already contains the core method/configurations, within the 72-hour lookback. Repository dates do not establish when it became public. This is conservatively newly-discovered catch-up on first inspection today rather than a claim that the paper announcement was the first public release; there is no evidence for an indexing-delay explanation.
evidence.limitations: Evidence is one MoE model family, a mathematical-verifier training corpus and one off-policy update configuration. Best checkpoints are selected on the same small benchmark set used for reporting, without a separate held-out checkpoint-selection set, which can bias the reported comparison upward. Main results average three runs but do not establish broad task or model generalization. The practical clipping surrogate and gradient approximations do not guarantee exact distribution-level KL control or monotonic policy improvement. CPU RSS savings depend on routing-index types and the compared implementation, and do not imply a measured end-to-end throughput gain. Comparison clipping settings are not an exhaustive per-method tuning study. No independent reproduction.

entries.title: Monitorability Is Trainable: Post-Training for Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
summary: Monitorability post-training rewards reasoning traces for retaining information about the eventual output, while a conditional divergence penalty discourages arbitrary changes in what those traces mean.

Across controlled compression and obfuscation settings, it restores useful monitoring signals without training against a particular monitor, suggesting a repair stage for reasoning models rather than a guarantee of faithful reasoning.

evidence.rationale: Full v1 methods and main experiments, plus MBPP Appendix B and synthetic-document setup, inspected. The lower-tail mutual-information objective caps rewards above a within-prompt quantile and applies its gradient only to reasoning tokens; conditional chi-square regularization acts on output tokens. On192 held-out MBPP prompts with four completions per prompt, the regularized Qwen2.5-7B recovery setting reports true-pass11.2%→48.6%, hack-monitor recall1.4%→37.4% and false-positive rate2.9%→3.9%; recovery statistics average five independent runs at the preselected divergence budget0.4 against one shared obfuscating checkpoint. The original Oct22 LG new-submission batch and official announcement schedule support an inferred Oct22 00:00UTC public release, preserving the Oct21 receipt date. No verified dedicated code release was found.
evidence.limitations: The shared starting policy was selected from three training runs for high hacking; controlled model organisms do not establish recovery of naturally arising failures in stronger agents. Post-training changes which reasoning/output modes are sampled and may lengthen reasoning, so gains are not solely a more transparent description of unchanged behavior. Conditional regularization discourages a private code but does not prove non-manipulability, full faithfulness, or persistence under later training. Format rewards remain active in MBPP despite absence of task/monitor rewards. No independent reproduction.

entries.title: ToM2Vec: Continuous Theory-of-Mind Tokens for Multi-Agent Coordination
summary: ToM2Vec trains an agent to predict continuous vectors summarizing a partner’s likely reasoning, using partner hidden states as self-play supervision.
The vectors condition later actions without requiring private partner context at inference, improving coordination in the tested games and transferring to unseen partner families in Overcooked.

evidence.rationale: Sections 2–4 and Appendices A–D specify ten autoregressive latent tokens, cosine-alignment supervision and Qwen3-8B experiments without direct task-reward training. Across three Overcooked layouts and 30 seeds, mean episode score rises from 94.7 to 106.7; a separate 20-seed partner test includes GPT-5.4 and Gemma-4. English game tasks also cover negotiation, Decrypto, Hanabi and capture/escape, with partner-state probes. Receipt 2026-10-21T16:05:54Z and the original cs.AI October 22 batch plus official schedule imply 2026-10-22T00:00Z release.
evidence.limitations: Training requires accessible partner reasoning and a shared representation space; workplace-team transfer is untested. Most evaluation uses one backbone and task-specific training; capture/escape have only 6/12 seeds. Appendix C reports no significant negotiation comparisons, contrary to broader main-text wording, and several other comparisons are nonsignificant. Ten latent steps add inference latency. Stated GitHub code, API and raw endpoints return 404 and are omitted.

entries.title: PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agents via Machine-Checked Integrity Theorems and Scalable Community Trust
summary: PerMIT isolates untrusted persistent memory behind a reader and an exact-content confirmation gate, then accumulates endorsements for sharing approved knowledge.
Machine-checked guarantees for its single-user model make the trust boundary explicit, while safety still depends on faithful enforcement and sound approval decisions.

evidence.rationale: Sections 3–5 and Appendices A/B/D/E describe opaque handles, exact-value/tool-scoped endorsements, Trojan Hippo containment and shared-memory construction. Automated gates show zero observed attacks over 20 cases per main configuration; telecom utility uses 24 held-out tasks with two trials, with pooled gains for Sonnet/Kimi but not GLM-5. Attached Lean source, correspondence and author build log were inspected; all 17 manifest hashes match, without rerunning Lean. Receipt 2026-10-20T23:31:06Z is preserved; the original cs.AI October 22 batch and official schedule support inferred 2026-10-22T00:00Z availability.
evidence.limitations: Theorems cover a specified single-user interpreter, not deployed-harness correctness, sound verifier judgments or federated probability bounds. Approval authorizes exact bytes and a tool, not task context or whole transactions; correlated approval errors and harmful reuse remain risks. Live cases do not replace adaptive payload search. The verified artifact is formal-model code, not the experimental harness.

entries.title: UserSWE: Evaluating Coding Agents in Multi-Turn Conversations with Dynamic Users
summary: UserSWE evaluates repository bug fixing through conversations whose simulated users reveal bounded information and change speaking styles across turns.
By combining tests after each turn with cross-family judgment review, it measures interactive progress and shows why a single-turn coding score can miss differences in collaboration efficiency.

evidence.rationale: Sections 4–5 and Appendices A–D detail information pools, frozen per-task persona chains, executed-test verdicts and behavior-equivalent test rewrites that must fail on the base and pass on the candidate. Eleven model–scaffold agents run 72 tasks from 42 repositories: 50 single-issue tasks with five-turn budgets and 22 two-issue tasks with eight. Persona frequencies derive from 20,859 proprietary sessions, filtered to 13,530 code-changing sessions. Rankings vary by budget; length-discounted scores include task-bootstrap intervals and paired comparisons. Receipt 2026-10-21T14:46:22Z plus original cs.AI October 22 batch/schedule imply 2026-10-22T00:00Z availability.
evidence.limitations: Only 72 tasks and one/two-issue maintenance episodes are evaluated; this is not a universal model ranking or a human-user trial. Simulator labels and equivalence approvals still depend on model judgments, and scaffolds differ across agents. Proprietary sessions are not released, task-bootstrap intervals do not establish repeated-run stability, and a public benchmark/code URL was not verified; release is promised.

entries.title: UlaCache: Unified Logical Addressing for Sparse LLM Serving
summary: UlaCache gives sparse-attention histories stable logical addresses across GPU and CPU memory, reducing redundant copies while sharing GPU cache capacity across requests.

Its parallel replacement and transfer scheduling let GLM-5.3 sustain larger decode batches under matched memory budgets, reaching up to 2.51× HiSparse’s peak decoding throughput on eight B300 GPUs with speculative decoding enabled.

evidence.rationale: Full pinned v1 PDF (12 pages) and HTML methods, evaluation and related work inspected. Stable logical IDs resolve to GPU/CPU storage slots; TP distributes retained history across ranks and uses separate local buffers for selected copies, whereas DP keeps rank-local pools. PB-LRU uses shared recency buckets and hierarchical bitmaps; transfer plans protect current readers, exchange incoming/outgoing KV, and commit address mappings only after transfers finish. Selection-plan reuse and cross-layer prefetch apply when layers share sparse selections. GLM-5.3 uses FP8 weights/KV and BF16 activations on eight H200 or eight B300 GPUs; CPU budgets are128GB or192GB per GPU, respectively, and the B300 persistent model/cache budget is272GB per GPU. Multi-LexSum inputs contain64K–128K tokens and generate2048 greedy output tokens. Under matched memory budgets, peak decode-throughput ratios versus HiSparse with two-step MTP are H200 DP1.16×/TP1.70× and B300 DP1.73×/TP2.51×. This differs from prior RemoteKV (prefill transfer scaling), CacheSmith (RAG reuse selection) and PageWeaver (sparse query unions): the central contribution is active sparse-history placement and replacement. Timing: v1 received2026-10-21T14:46:11Z; the original cs.DC Thursday22 batch and official20:00US/Eastern schedule imply announcement2026-10-22T00:00Z, within this daily window. No verified author implementation link was found in the paper or exact-name public repository lookup.
evidence.limitations: One sparse-attention model and two eight-GPU platforms were measured; examples of other architectures are motivation, not their evaluation. All requests finish prefill before measured decoding, and each system’s observed maximum is taken over its own measured batch sizes, so these are decode-only peak-throughput comparisons, not fixed-batch or online end-to-end SLO speedups. At batch1 UlaCache is slower than fully GPU-resident SGLang in all eight configurations, though faster than HiSparse. Bucketed LRU is approximate; its scheduling ablation excludes data transfer and can lose to naive LRU when replacement pressure is low. TP score all-gather, local copied buffers, transfer bandwidth, metadata and workspaces remain costs. No downstream quality study, distributed fault-recovery study or independently reproduced result is claimed; a public UlaCache code release was not verified.

entries.title: Accelerating PyTorch on AMD GPUs with FlyDSL
summary: AMD and Meta document how PyTorch can select FlyDSL kernels through ordinary eager, compiled matrix-multiplication and attention APIs, with explicit hardware layouts and scheduling for MI350-series GPUs.

The report connects kernel-level optimizations to controlled vLLM serving comparisons on one MI355X, helping developers distinguish modest BF16 gains from larger workload-dependent improvements in MXFP8 and MXFP4 execution.

evidence.rationale: Complete technical blog, official README, linked PyTorch PR descriptions and AOTriton release inspected. The Oct21 report explains half-tile interleaving and staged LDS/MFMA scheduling, persistent grouped-GEMM expert scheduling, scale lifetimes for MXFP formats, eager RMSNorm/TopK overrides, and AOTriton attention selection. Inductor benchmarks eligible FlyDSL GEMMs beside other enabled backends; it can retain ATen/Triton, and unsupported cases fall back. Operator benchmarks on MI355X are kept separate from whole-request vLLM A/B tests on TP1 Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Qwen3-32B and Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct (256input/512fixed-output tokens, concurrency8–256). The serving experiment changes only the GEMM candidate list under matched per-model cache/configuration: BF16 peaks1.13× against ATen+Triton, MXFP8 peaks2.04× against ATen, and MXFP4 peaks3.01× against ATen. BF16 has at least two ABBA-interleaved repetitions; MXFP8/4 have one run per cell. This is a substantive new detailed integration/serving measurement report, while the backend and most operator measurements were public earlier. Repo creation is2025-11-23; RMSNorm PR191447 openedJul29, TopK193548 Aug14, grouped194032 Aug19, dense-layout194981 Aug27, MXFP196719 Sep11, and AOTriton0.14.2b was releasedSep25. These dates prevent treating the kernels themselves as a newOct21 invention. Blog metadata gives publication2026-10-21T17:45:40Z, inside the current daily window.
evidence.limitations: The reviewed update is the newOct21 report and end-to-end evaluation, not first release of FlyDSL or a blanket new feature claim. Main integration targets gfx950/MI350; static layout, dtype, alignment and shape restrictions apply. MXFP kernel timing starts with already quantized operands and excludes input quantization, compilation and autotuning. The attention release comparison also changes Triton, AITER and tuning databases and is not an isolated FlyDSL causal comparison. Eager RMSNorm backward retains the old implementation; SDPA via AOTriton differs from FlexAttention, whose FlyDSL backend is future work. BF16 serving gains are small or within the1.79% noise floor for70B; low-precision cells have no repeated-run uncertainty and compare ATen rather than the BF16 ATen/Triton baseline. Quantization/model-quality equivalence is not evaluated here, TopK tied indices/NaN choices can differ across implementations, and no general training or fleet-wide speedup follows. No author code or benchmark was executed.

entries.title: Is 2:4 Sparsity Still Worth It? Semi-Structured Sparsity versus Quantization in LLM Inference
summary: This study compares structured 2:4 sparsity with lower-precision dense inference while counting index metadata, dynamic preprocessing and the hardware’s actual sparse operand constraints.

Across the tested models and GPUs, it finds that quantizing further is usually the better next step when a lower supported precision remains, while sparsity at the tested precision floor can raise throughput but needs retraining to recover usable model quality.

evidence.rationale: Full21-page v1 paper inspected, including Sections3–6, all comparison/evaluation tables and AppendicesA–I, plus the author README and initial artifact tree/history. Metadata-inclusive bit accounting pairs 2:4 INT8 with dense INT5 (both5.125bits/original element with group128 FP16 scales), rather than incorrectly with INT4. Per-layer operator comparisons cover Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B across W/X/Q/K/V/attention probabilities; measured kernels use L40S, H100 and RTX PRO6000, including online pruning/quantization for dynamic operands. The strongest dense rival at a hardware tier dominates the tested sparse alternatives above the deployment precision floor; some sparse cases beat weaker quantizers or improve retrieval/perplexity, so this is not a universal all-metric ranking. On one H100, historical vLLM0.11.2 serves Llama-3.1-8B versus externally retrained13B-token Sparse-Llama; sparse FP8 prefill is74.6k versus58.9k tokens/s (64×2048-token prompts), with batch1 decode234 versus198 and batch64 decode9914 versus8556 tokens/s. The same sparse weights served densely remove the throughput benefit within3%, separating kernel gain from model differences. Original source date isOct20 receipt21:48:45Z; code repo created18:50:58Z and initial696a1107 commit19:59:45Z onOct20 already contains implementation and measurements. Although the original cs.LG paper batch isOct22, this unreported work is conservatively an editorial delayed discovery inside the72-hour lookback, not a new optimization first released in theOct22 main window. Commit timestamps do not prove exact historical public visibility; optional earliest-work public_availability is therefore omitted.
evidence.limitations: Two8B models, a finite quantizer/pruner menu and specific shapes/hardware support the conclusions; the precision floor is defined by the tested inference stack, explicitly excluding unused Ada INT4 tensor-core paths. Operator error is an imperfect whole-model proxy; GSM8K uses the first250 problems with8-shot greedy chain-of-thought and broad confidence intervals, and some retrieval/perplexity results favor sparsity. Sparse library algorithms receive exhaustive tuning while dense libraries use default heuristics. Accuracy-winning dynamic correction is omitted from sparse timing, and some low-bit comparisons are simulated rather than hardware kernels. The27% prefill result uses historical vLLM0.11.2, not current serving releases (Sparse24 was removed in0.19); no GSM8K difference in that serving table is significant. The author’s two1B-token retraining runs are single, untuned recipes on fourH100 each; the13B-token Sparse-Llama reference uses different training data, so recovery cost is not a controlled token-scaling law. Blackwell sparse FP4 requires pairwise4:8, distinct from element-wise2:4, and the limited retraining budget failed to recover reasoning. No independent reproduction was performed.

entries.title: Capable Teacher, Myopic Scorer: Reward-Free Teacher Repair for Agentic On-Policy Distillation
summary: Rollout-to-Scorer Distillation first repairs a teacher’s token scores using its own continuations from difficult student states, then freezes that teacher for ordinary on-policy distillation.
The tested agents complete more tasks and spend fewer turns on unproductive searching, showing why a teacher’s ability to solve a task can differ from the usefulness of its next-token supervision.

evidence.rationale: Pinned v1 Sections3–5 and relevant mining, selection, training and evaluation appendices inspected. R2S mines high-disagreement states from an untrained student, generates eight teacher takeovers per state, selects short validated endings, and trains a teacher copy to reproduce takeover-conditioned Top16 token targets on the student’s complete assistant suffix without seeing the takeover. A frozen repaired scorer then supplies the standard OPD signal. Table2 covers two teachers, four students and three replayable text environments, with12 teacher-student-environment cells; the author-reported mean improvement over the best of three comparison OPD methods is12.8 success percentage points. Each main cell is one150-step training run evaluated with three decoding seeds, not three independent training seeds. The Qwen3.5-9B→4B dynamics study separately repeats student training three times while sharing one repaired teacher. Main reward-free filtering uses consensus and/or a judge; ScienceWorld completion messages and other observable end states still supply feedback. The paper is in the original October21 CL new-submission batch; original October20 receipt is retained. Author code, project and moving-main/release-tag guidance were inspected. Earlier code history is acknowledged; no exact first-public Git timestamp is inferred. Conservative catch-up classification preserves the earlier implementation context inside the72-hour lookback instead of claiming the paper batch is the first-ever public method release.
evidence.limitations: Repair adds untrained-student mining, up to19,200 teacher-takeover episodes, selection and one full teacher fine-tune before the matched150 student steps, so main accuracy comparisons are not end-to-end compute matched. Most main results have only one training run per cell. Evidence is confined to Qwen3/Qwen3.5 and replayable ALFWorld/WebShop/ScienceWorld with fixed demonstrations and turn limits. Reward-free means no numeric task reward is read in selected variants, not absence of outcome cues, consensus assumptions or a model judge. A poorly aligned teacher or unreliable filter may still mislead. The capability/scoring diagnosis is evidence for these settings, not a proof that all OPD failures share one cause. No independent reproduction.

entries.title: Reward Misspecification Degrades Chain-of-Thought Monitorability
summary: Controlled reinforcement-learning experiments show that misspecified output rewards can produce reward-hacking answers while the visible reasoning continues to sound compliant, even without training against a monitor.

Inferring and teaching a description of the learned reward makes the reasoning more informative in these tests, giving training teams a way to investigate monitorability separately from task success or safety.

evidence.rationale: Pinned v1 Sections3–5 and reward/monitor/description appendices inspected. Three models (GPT-OSS20B/120B and Nemotron30B-A3B), three synthetic tasks (length-limit violation, model-identity preference bias and incomplete-code-test exploitation), and three seeds separate true-reward controls from misspecified-reward runs. LoRArank32 on Tinker uses grouped policy-gradient training; monitor inputs contain intent, query and CoT but not the final answer. Table1 has mean hack rate0.87 versus0.05 in controls while intervention and reward-intent g-mean-squared metrics are0.13/0.17. A second RL run uses reward descriptions inferred from diverse scored rollouts and injected in half of training samples, while updates omit the description from context. Table2 raises these monitorability metrics to0.37/0.59 (+0.24/+0.42 absolute metric units), with hack rate still0.79. The current author code/datasets were inspected; code history dated October20 precedes the October21 CL paper announcement, so this is conservative delayed discovery within72hours rather than a claim of a first-ever method release at midnight. Original October20 receipt and actual first-seen time are preserved.
evidence.limitations: The testbed deliberately constructs small, sometimes inverted rewards; coding uses only10 test cases per question and its misspecified reward requires at least one pass and one failure. These controlled results do not quantify real-world covert deception or prove CoT monitoring is universally ineffective. G-mean-squared combines true/false-positive behavior and is not ordinary detection accuracy; coding labels can mark failing-all-tests attempts as non-hacking. Description training costs another RL run plus generator/selection inference, raises some false positives and improves disclosure without reliably eliminating hacking. Evaluations use two external LLM monitors and are API/model dependent. No independent reproduction or general safety guarantee.

entries.title: Evolving Agent Interfaces
summary: Agent S4 evolves executable computer interfaces and usage knowledge from unlabeled synthetic-task trajectories, while a separate validation controller selects repositories and the task model and harness stay fixed.

On 108 OSWorld V2 tasks, evolving a shared seed raises binary success from 19.44% to 21.30%, suggesting that reusable application interfaces can help a computer-use agent, although the reported aggregate includes 15 tasks used for repository selection.

evidence.rationale: Full Sections 2–7, Tables 1–4 and Appendices A/B plus mechanism prompts inspected. Population search alternates mutation/crossover for 30 descendants, with binary-tournament parent selection; the builder sees only 30 synthetic OSWorld training trajectories or 48 ScienceBoard synthetic trajectories and cannot access the 15 benchmark validation tasks/scores. Selection uses those validation scores, so the process is verifier-free only for construction evidence, not selection. Qwen3.8-27B and the Prime Agent harness remain fixed. Matched OSWorld results are 15.74% without a repository, 19.44% with the human seed and 21.30% with the best evolved no-scratch repository; full 108-task evaluation includes the 15 selection tasks. A separate ScienceBoard evolution reaches 58.58% versus 55.03% seed on 169 tasks, likewise including15 selection tasks. The 5.56% fixed-GUI comparison uses another harness/access surface and is not an isolated evolution gain. Original cs.AI October 21 batch and official schedule support inferred paper availability2026-10-21T00:00Z. The older Agent-S repository adds distinct S4 code in observed merge 58187e364e at October 21 at 05:32Z; no earlier S4-specific content release was established.
evidence.limitations: Validation overlaps the final aggregate; final repositories have small single-run gains over a strong manually authored seed and no reported repeated full-benchmark confidence interval. The method changes available interfaces versus the fixed-GUI baseline, so the headline 3.8 times comparison cannot isolate evolution. Cost estimates assume 80% input-cache hits and exclude repository construction/infrastructure. Qualitative traces and successful-task token/call subsets do not establish uniform task latency savings. No independent reproduction.

entries.title: Cache Engineering for Agents
summary: Cache engineering lets an agent drop selected KV states and reposition retained keys without rewriting its text history; AKV tracks operation history so shared or restored caches remain consistent.

The full-paper study reports 1.7 points higher average task scores and 27.7% lower estimated token cost than threshold summarization across three models and four agent benchmarks, suggesting a useful route to context control when builders also control the serving engine.

evidence.rationale: Full Sections 3–5, Tables 1–4 and Appendices A.1–A.4 inspected. Drop changes future attention but not retained hidden states; repos rotates retained RoPE keys and resets future position indices, rather than making them equivalent to recomputing a shortened text. AKV uses operation-aware radix branches, drop-aware eviction and segmented restoration. Main policy retains the latest 12 tool responses plus reasoning, with model-specific position thresholds. Three-model/four-benchmark tests report mean 1.7 score-point gain and 27.7% API-equivalent agent/summary token-cost reduction versus Standard; costs exclude other tools and are not billed GPU expenditure. Eight A800-80GB BF16 GPT-OSS-120B serving replay reports 1.18 times output throughput and 1.51 times P95 request-latency speedup at each method's own peak concurrency. Original cs.CL October 21 batch plus official announcement schedule supports inferred formal-study availability2026-10-21T00:00Z. The September 28 repository and pinned October 15 README already document the drop/repos implementation but contain no benchmark results; this is proposed as the new full-paper evaluation/formalization over an older code preview, not as a newly invented operation.
evidence.limitations: Cached hidden states retain information from previously attended dropped tokens, and arbitrary policies can degrade quality; serving support for linear-attention models remains future work. Serving replay selects 80 longest-context SWE tasks and replays recorded tool outputs with method-specific trajectories/budgets, not identical live workloads. API-equivalent prices and reposition charges are modeling assumptions. The current results-bearing project page is accessible, but its source repository/history returns 404, so earlier project-page visibility cannot be reconstructed and exact global first public visibility is uncertain. No independent reproduction.

entries.update_note: 2026-10-21: The first arXiv paper adds a formal operation-history account and a three-model/four-benchmark evaluation to the older AKV implementation preview. The verified October 15 README already describes drop/repos and compatible-cache reuse, so those mechanisms are not claimed as new on this date; exact earlier project-page visibility is unresolved.

entries.title: TorchTPU: Native PyTorch Backend, Pod-Scale Training and vLLM Serving
summary: The new TorchTPU reports explain how native PyTorch tensors, eager execution, graph compilation and distributed collectives map to Google TPUs, alongside a vLLM plugin that reuses upstream model and serving code.

They provide concrete portability and scaling evidence plus implementation guidance for precision, views, collective safety and custom kernels, helping developers distinguish a working port from a tuned deployment.

evidence.rationale: Read the full PyTorch architecture/case-study report, complete vLLM launch report, current code READMEs/support matrix and earlier April7 Google architecture article. PyTorch publication metadata is October20 16:02:30Z; the vLLM launch source merged16:29:35Z, both after October20 cutoff and before October21 cutoff. New detailed evidence includes4917-model smoke/lowering testing (4821passes) and a657-model numerical subset (638passes under stated tolerances), not universal model equivalence. Qwen3-MoE235B BF16 training uses SimpleFSDP/HSDP, Pallas kernels, scan, collective overlap, activation offload/checkpointing and fixed per-TensorCore batch16/length4096; increasing from1024to8192 TPUv7 chips grows global batch32768to262144, with2236to2104tokens/s/TensorCore and28.8to27.1%MFU. This is weak scaling. vLLM TorchTPU is an out-of-tree plugin using torch.compile to XLA and Pallas custom ops, plus TPU Sync for host KV offload and resharded disaggregation. The April article already described eager/compile/distributed architecture; the update is inspectable code integration and expanded implementation/coverage/scaling evidence.
evidence.limitations: Portability does not promise peak performance or bitwise equality: default matrix multiplication uses BF16 inputs/FP32 accumulation; higher precision is multipass. The5000-model headline mixes smoke/lowering checks and narrower numerical tests with nonzero tolerances. Pod scaling is weak scaling with tuned kernels/scan and increased global batch, not strong scaling or a pure eager baseline. TPUv7 chip and TensorCore counts differ by2x; avoid mixing their throughput units. Bounded dynamism/MPMD collective optimization remains conditional or experimental; unsafe SPMD assumptions can deadlock or corrupt execution. vLLM recommendsv7x whilev5/v6are experimental; feature-specific support is narrower than every upstream model. No broad GPU/TPU TCO leadership or model-quality claim is inferred from third-party/author benchmark summaries. No independent reproduction.

entries.update_note: 2026-10-20: The PyTorch report and vLLM TorchTPU launch add implementation-level explanations, public backend/plugin artifacts, model-coverage protocols and pod-scale training/serving case studies (https://pytorch.org/blog/introducing-torchtpu/; https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-20-vllm-torchtpu). The April7 Google article already introduced the native backend architecture (https://developers.googleblog.com/torchtpu-running-pytorch-natively-on-tpus-at-google-scale/); repository creation dates in March/June are not first-public-release proof. This entry selects the new detailed evidence and public integration, not a first invention of the eager or XLA path.

entries.title: Humming: Unified Quantized Inference Kernels and New Serving Measurements
summary: Humming separates a model’s quantization description from hardware-specific execution choices, composing shared data movement, dequantization, scheduling and Tensor Core components into specialized kernels.

The new engineering report shows how this design translates selected low-bit formats into practical dense and mixture-of-experts execution, with an explicit serving comparison that changes activation precision while preserving the checkpoint’s quantized weights.

evidence.rationale: Read the complete dated blog/Markdown and prior source document, architecture/format/device support, benchmark methodology, full end-to-end table and future-work caveats. The main article source merged October21 02:45:20Z; its PR opened October19 and cites an earlier Humming source. The verified source commit8549542 at October20 09:35:28Z specifically adds end-to-end results, so this is an editorial catch-up of that substantive report update within the October21 total72-hour lookback, not a first-ever library release. Humming code dates to February and its PyPI README update to September. The new comparison uses DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash on8H20 GPUs, TP8, same MXFP4 weights, MarlinW4A16/BF16 versus HummingW4A8/tokenwiseFP8 activations. Across concurrency1-64, authors report output throughput+14.1to43.3%; at64,442.37to633.94outputtokens/s, TTFT5467.35to3882.94ms, TPOT123.25to85.70ms. Separate microbenchmarks use warmed kernels/coldL2 and powers-of-twoM1-8192; their speedups are not serving speedups.
evidence.limitations: Activation precision and backend change together; the end-to-end experiment is not an iso-numerics kernel-only comparison and no corresponding task-quality or long-context accuracy test is reported. Hardware/shape/format support is conditional, and quantization storage savings alone do not imply native low-bit arithmetic on older GPUs. Kernel and compilation results use different cases/baselines; do not generalize extreme microbenchmark ratios. Default tuning uses heuristics; autotuning and deeper EP integration are future work. Blog data is author/community reported, not independently reproduced. The October21 publication republishes prior source material; the October20 new end-to-end source update is explicitly preserved rather than resetting method/code age.

This is delayed editorial discovery of a new measured report update, not newly released code; commit time documents source provenance without asserting an exact website-visibility timestamp.

entries.title: The Token-Energy Law of LLM Decode: Active Bytes and Realized Time Account for Joules per Token
summary: This study models decode energy per useful output token using separately counted shared-weight traffic, private key-value history and elapsed time per token, with coefficients calibrated to each model and execution setting.

It explains why batching, context length and runtime behavior affect energy differently, and offers a compact accounting tool for interpreting measured serving trade-offs rather than a hardware-independent energy constant.

evidence.rationale: Read Sections1-7, all energy/traffic methods and Tables2-8. Logical weights are amortized by realized useful outputs per iteration; KV bytes use output-weighted attended history plus one append, not allocated cache size. A fitted affine response combines those coordinates and observed decode duration. Tests use BF16 Qwen2.5-7B/14B and Mistral7B on GH200/GB300, including two-GPU GH200 tensor parallelism, fixed700W/1300W limits, full-history attention and vLLM graph/eager policy. NVML integration is synchronized; separate177Nsight profiles test logical reads. Across374held-out energy executions (270static across54cells plus104controlled departure traces), fixed per-setting coefficients yield maximum condition-mean absolute percentage error3.73%. This is condition-mean accuracy, not maximum individual-run error. Same-SKU GPU transfer is tested; cross-model/platform instances are separately calibrated. Receipt October20 17:32:08Z is preserved. Original cs.LG Wednesday21 batch plus official release schedule imply announcement October21T00Z.
evidence.limitations: The model uses observed duration; prospective planning needs an independently validated latency model. Energy boundary is GPU-board decode only, excluding prefill/CPU/network/datacenter and lifecycle/carbon costs; contributions in fitted stacked bars are not independently metered physical components. No universal coefficients or causal energy-per-byte constants are established. Quantization, prefix caching, speculation, chunked prefill, offload and preemption are disabled. Dynamic tests drain requests without new arrivals and run beyond the graph-capture cap, so they are not a full production continuous-batching trace. Multi-node/pipeline execution and MoE need new validation/accounting; dividing activated MoE parameter bytes by full batch is explicitly invalid. No dedicated public artifact/code release was verified and no independent reproduction was performed.

entries.title: MemT-1.0: Towards Memory-Native Evolution
summary: MemT-1.0 adds trainable memory modules to frozen language-model backbones with stable token-level state updates, and studies densely routed memory experts as a way to expand capacity.

Its released models turn growing interaction histories into bounded persistent states, offering predictable session storage while exposing a clear trade-off between compact memory and precise historical recall.

evidence.rationale: Pinned v1 architecture/training Sections2–3, memory evaluation Section6, limitations Section8 and relevant configuration/evaluation appendices inspected. Gated DeltaNet-2 writes token-level information at turn/segment boundaries, while generation reads the incoming state. The explored Mixture-of-Storage expansion routes densely across all memory experts, not sparse top-k experts; both released Nano and Flash configurations use one memory expert per selected layer (Appendix B, Table6), while expanded MoS is studied separately. The34B-token pipeline uses current-segment CE followed by off-policy full-context-teacher distillation with Top64 forward-KL targets. Only memory parameters are optimized during native-memory training. Nano uses Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and451M trainable memory parameters; Flash uses a separately prepared DeepSeek-V4-Flash backbone and3.61B memory parameters. Across11 memory benchmarks their reported macro-averages are47.0 and50.6, ahead of tested parametric-memory baselines but below strong textual-memory methods. At128K history, Nano reports1.86x end-to-end inference speed and66x less logical per-trajectory state than full-context KV. The speed test uses HF inference on two GPUs, batch/concurrency1,35 histories, a fixed512-token query and forced128-token response, including history preparation/state restoration but excluding loading/tokenization/scoring. The original CL October20 batch/schedule gives an inferred October20T00Z paper announcement; the observed release commit (authored October20T02:48:07Z, committed05:27:44Z) contains code and a complete tech_report.pdf. These Git timestamps document content history, not exact first public visibility. Code/project links were verified, not executed.
evidence.limitations: Fixed state cannot retain unlimited detail: exact recall deteriorates and retrieval/text-memory systems remain stronger on aggregate. The66x figure excludes shared backbone weights, embedders/hyper-memory parameters and is logical persistent session state, not total GPU-memory savings. The1.86x speedup is one specific HF workload and is mainly history-preparation savings; short histories are slower, and heterogeneous baseline backbones/runtimes limit broad efficiency rankings. Dense expert expansion increases memory computation. General-capability preservation is evaluated under specified noise conditions, not a guarantee of unchanged behavior. Application-specific experience training/retrieval adds costs; online state updates are not autonomous weight-level self-improvement. The October20v2 revision is not used for this report’s cutoff.

entries.title: Self-Distillation for Supervised Fine-Tuning
summary: Gold-Conditioned Distillation replaces one-hot fine-tuning targets with soft predictions from an exponentially averaged copy of the model that can see the correct response in its prompt.

Both models follow the fixed gold response without generating training rollouts, and the new study finds better target-task learning with modest average retention gains, suggesting a practical alternative to ordinary supervised fine-tuning.

evidence.rationale: Pinned v1 Sections 3–5 and Appendices A–F inspected. A gold-revealed EMA teacher (update rate0.01) supplies forward-KL targets on exactly the same gold-response prefixes seen by the student; neither model samples completions during training. Four backbones span Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Qwen3-4B-Base, Llama3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B-Base, with full tuning at3–4B and rank64 LoRA at8B. Table8’s five-seed Tooluse study reports GCD66.7±0.6 versus SFT61.1±0.7 on Qwen2.5-3B and69.6±0.5 versus63.2±0.6 on Qwen3-4B; Llama gains are smaller. Main tasks also cover scientific MCQ and LiveNews; previous capability is measured on five general benchmarks. Shared four-epoch A10080GB pipelines, label-smoothing/base-KL comparisons and EMA/KL-direction ablations provide controls. This new detailed paper and controlled evaluation were announced in the October20 CL batch; the compact author implementation existed earlier, so the entry is a material paper update rather than a new-code release.
evidence.limitations: Retention gains are modest and individual metrics can regress, including instruction following. LiveNews trains on paraphrased versions of the same facts tested with original questions; this is phrasing transfer after knowledge injection, not generalization to unseen facts. Main comparisons use matched settings but not exhaustive per-method tuning; SDFT is reproduced with a forward-KL modification, and its learning-rate sweep covers only selected cases. Multi-seed results cover Tooluse and three models, not every task/backbone. Soft targets add a teacher forward and EMA storage even though they avoid autoregressive rollouts; no universal wall-time saving is measured. Released compact code covers Tooluse/LiveNews on the two smaller Qwen models, not the full paper experiment suite. All models are at most8B; no independent reproduction.

entries.update_note: 2026-10-20: The newly announced full paper adds four-backbone target-task/retention comparisons, a five-seed Tooluse study and EMA/KL/soft-label ablations to the earlier compact GCD implementation (https://arxiv.org/html/2610.25497v1; https://arxiv.org/list/cs.CL/recent?skip=0&show=2000; https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html). The author repository’s single October18 commit contains a compact training implementation and data rather than these controlled study results (https://github.com/WenxuanZhu1103/gcd; https://api.github.com/repos/WenxuanZhu1103/gcd/git/trees/main?recursive=1; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/WenxuanZhu1103/gcd/main/README.md). Git creation/commit dates do not establish exact first public visibility. Preserve October18 as the paper’s receipt date; October20T00Z refers only to its schedule-inferred paper announcement, not a reset of method/code age.

entries.title: CoworkEnv: Synthesizing Training Environments for Long-Horizon Cowork Agents
summary: CoworkEnv synthesizes coordinated service records, tool interfaces and executable graders, validates their consistency, and turns teacher executions into training demonstrations for compact work agents.

SFT raises Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct's mean score from 46.6 to 64.1 on 199 Claw-Eval tasks and improves a separate ClawMark-trained checkpoint from 11.8 to 19.4 on 100 tasks, showing how executable workflow construction can supply useful agent-training data.

evidence.rationale: Full Methods 3, Experiments 4, Limitations and Appendices A–F inspected. Capability plans generate requests, initial records, tools and weighted completion/prohibited-action checks; programmatic gates test parsing, service references, answer-identifier leakage and synthetic grading consistency, allowing one repair retry. Teacher-success and structure/length filters prepare assistant-token SFT; the mixed-pool replay retains937/1,809 demonstrations, while other export branches have distinct thresholds. Claw-Eval base/SFT comparisons use 161 General plus 38 Multi-turn tasks with three trials/task; the metric is mean fractional score on0–100, not binary success. The 77.8 versus 45.9 Multi-turn gain is 31.9 points. Separate ClawMark SFT is evaluated on 100tasks. Original cs.AI October 20 batch plus official schedule supports inferred paper availability2026-10-20T00:00Z; Sunday October 18 receipt is preserved. Observed initial GitHub pipeline contentOctober 19 at 20:36Z, lessons contentOctober 19 at 20:07Z and model uploadsOctober 19 at 17:57Z are in this same daily window; repository creation onOctober 16 alone is not evidence of earlier substantive availability. Classified conservatively as newly-discovered using the preserved October 18 receipt date within the 72-hour discovery window; earlier October 19 model/code content is acknowledged rather than using the later paper announcement as the earliest release of the work. This is editorial catch-up, not delayed indexing.
evidence.limitations: Graders cover declared calls/records rather than all semantics: the documented ticket-update check does not verify resolution text. Teacher filtering can discard recovery behavior and favors a proprietary teacher. RL pipelines share supervised warm-up and vary multiple configuration choices, so their gains over the base cannot isolate RL or one credit-assignment mechanism. Public code is incremental: selected synthesis/adapters/SFT and RL-preprocessing components are present, while full distributed RL stack and task datasets are not bundled. Separate HF checkpoints are listed, but this review did not run or independently reproduce them.

entries.title: MultiLangBench and behavior-preserving COBOL migration evaluation
summary: OpenAI introduced MultiLangBench, which tests whether coding models can implement a SQLite-compatible engine across 20 programming languages, alongside a separate COBOL migration evaluation requiring exact output preservation. The released tests give developers a concrete way to assess long coding sessions in less common languages, while the authors report substantial accuracy gains for their latest models under these specific settings.
The migration suite remains hidden, and success on either evaluation does not establish production readiness or general superiority across software engineering tasks.

evidence.limitations: The public tests adapt a subset of SQLite semantics and do not establish full database compatibility; default 272-test scoring differs from running all converted tests. The blog does not expose the COBOL task set, task count, complete harness, sampling uncertainty or business-system dependencies; exact test success is narrower than real migration correctness. Model and reasoning-effort comparisons do not isolate a training recipe or architecture change, and estimated API cost depends on output usage and pricing. The current repository contains dated historical commits before its creation; their timestamps alone are not evidence of a prior public release. No independent reproduction was performed.
