evidence.rationale: Read the complete October 19 technical blog and public benchmark README, inspected the repository tree and three-commit history, and compared the initial README. The contribution is an inspectable cross-language database I/O contract plus newly reported 20-language and COBOL-migration results: an initial database and user SQL produce a candidate database that real SQLite 3.40.1 checks with a validation query. Of roughly 51k upstream TCL tests, roughly 24k were converted; the README specifies a 272-test hash-prefix subset by default, a 60-second test timeout, and joint reporting of API cost and pass rate. Authors report 87.4% mean MultiLangBench test pass rate for GPT-6 Astra at maximum reasoning effort versus 26.8% for GPT-5.6 Sol; the separate hidden COBOL suite counts a migration only when all byte-parity tests pass. This report backfills the October 20 window using actual October 21 discovery. The dated blog is the public-release source; imported September 29/October 6 commits do not prove earlier public visibility, and the current repository was created October 19.

entries.title: One Search, Two Layers: Compiler Controls Inside PyTorch Helion using NVIDIA CompileIQ
summary: This engineering study treats compiler control files as another tuning dimension alongside a kernel’s tile shapes, warp counts and pipeline settings, rather than stopping optimization at the kernel source.

It demonstrates a measured workflow for finding and pinning small additional gains in already tuned kernels, while validating numerical outputs and matching each control file to its hardware and compiler version.

evidence.rationale: Read the complete report including fixed/joint search, runtime/occupancy/multi-objective experiments and caveats. Article metadata gives publication October19 15:45:05Z, after the October19 cutoff and before October20 cutoff. The new experimental case uses a pre-tuned Helion NVFP4 decode GEMV on GB200/sm100, ptxas13.3.73, CUDA13.3, CompileIQ1.0.3 and Triton3.8.0, locked clocks and PyTorch-reference output checks. For N8192/K28672, fixed-kernel compiler-control search remeasures about0.0975to0.0930ms (1.048x); the joint runtime/L1TEX objective reports1.0689x with L1TEX throughput81.51to85.96%. Two-shape search reports about1.05x and1.01x on the respective validated shapes. Welch tests and effect-size filters are author-side repeated-timing checks. Helion ACF support existed March6, CompileIQ1.0 released May26, and booster packs existed May/August; this is selected as a new scoped experiment/workflow report, not a new compiler or integration release.
evidence.limitations: Kernel microbenchmark improvements do not establish end-to-end LLM speedup, broad model coverage or universal2-7% gains. Search multiplies compilation/measurement trials and is intended offline; no amortized whole-workload savings are measured. Compiler-control files are architecture/toolkit specific, and mismatched controls can cause wrong results or runtime errors. Correctness checks cover the supplied reference cases, not all shapes or full training convergence. CompileIQ is distributed under a proprietary NVIDIA EULA even though Helion is open source and generated ACFs are redistributable. Code was inspected, not executed; no independent reproduction.

entries.update_note: 2026-10-19: The new PyTorch report publishes controlled Helion NVFP4 GEMV compiler-control tuning experiments, including repeated validation, two-shape and multi-objective cases (https://pytorch.org/blog/one-search-two-layers-compiler-controls-inside-pytorch-helion-using-nvidia-compileiq/). It builds on earlier Helion ACF integration and CompileIQ releases (https://api.github.com/repos/pytorch/helion/commits?path=examples/acfs&per_page=10; https://api.github.com/repos/NVIDIA/CompileIQ/releases?per_page=10), rather than introducing either project for the first time.

entries.title: Koi: Evidence-Guided, Self-Calibrating Planning for Multi-Cloud, Heterogeneous LLM Inference Fleets
summary: Koi uses language-model agents to propose cluster-wide inference deployments, then relies on deterministic prediction, constraint checks and telemetry to select and revise the plan.

Its persistent graph of scoped hypotheses connects configuration choices to runtime bottlenecks, helping a heterogeneous fleet improve serving objectives while accounting for uncertainty, scarce capacity and migration cost.

evidence.rationale: Read full Sections4-7 and AppendicesA/B, the code README, repository tree and pre-window history. Five-minute planning ticks combine a fixed decision-mediator-outcome DAG, Beta evidence, CUSUM residual tests, scoped mechanism proposals, deterministic AIConfigurator-derived predictions and capacity-constrained selection. The new paper reports a3-hour104-GPU GCP fleet across3regions with H100-80GB/A100-80GB/A100-40GB/RTXPRO6000. Against the strongest evaluated real-cluster baseline, Table2 reports4119.51 versus3497.43 SLO-honoring output tokens/s (17.79% higher) and0.24 versus0.30 times10^-4 dollars per SLO-honoring output token (20% lower). These are fleet-capacity accounting costs; planner LLM cost is separate. The larger45%goodput/31%cost gains belong to a400-GPU3-hour simulation, not the real fleet. The full paper is the original cs.DC Tuesday20 announcement (inferred October20T00Z with official schedule); receipt October17 01:03:13Z is preserved. Earlier code and short README predate this paper; the inspected September17 commit tree has no paperPDF and README explicitly says whitepaper-coming-soon.
evidence.limitations: Causal edges are fixed, observational and scoped; their evidence confidence is not proof of identified causal effects. Near-optimal candidate coverage and convergence under stationary conditions are assumptions; the12-hour experiment did not reach convergence. Real hardware omits most non-evolutionary baselines because of cost; main baseline implementations are ports with their own static candidate restrictions, and AppendixB notes registration/reproducibility gaps. Simulation uses a separate execution simulator and must not be presented as real cluster evidence. A model-backbone gap is dominated by one batch admission/configuration decision with different hardware and replication, not an isolated model comparison. Code was read, not run; no independent reproduction.

entries.update_note: 2026-10-20: The newly announced full paper supplies formal scoring/evidence updates,104-GPU real-fleet evaluation, simulation and ablation accounting beyond the older Koi implementation and short preview (https://arxiv.org/html/2610.24355v1; https://github.com/Tandemn-Labs/tandemn-koi; https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Tandemn-Labs/tandemn-koi/4826bcee17104808793809a18031c9e3b5bbe028/README.md). The inspected repository was created March10 and has September17 implementation commits; dates document prior content, not exact public visibility. Original cs.DC Tuesday20 batch plus official schedule establish the inferred paper-update release (https://arxiv.org/list/cs.DC/recent?skip=0&show=2000; https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html). No earliest-work availability is reset to the paper date.

entries.title: A Stronger Teacher Within: Strengthening MoE Models via On-Policy Bidirectional Distillation
summary: MoEvolve temporarily activates more experts, repairs their cooperation by distilling from the original model, strengthens the expanded model with verifiable-reward training, and distills its gains back into the original expert budget.

Across four tested mixture-of-experts backbones, this produces stronger domain-specific models without increasing their final activation budget, offering a way to improve a model using its own latent capacity instead of an external stronger teacher.

evidence.rationale: Pinned v1 Sections 3–6 and relevant Appendices A–I inspected, including restoration, RL, reverse distillation, domain-specific evaluation and wall-clock accounting. OLMoE-1B-7B, DeepSeek-V2-Lite, GPT-OSS-20B and Qwen3-30B-A3B are each trained as separate mathematics, code and ScienceQA checkpoints. Expansion uses up to all available experts, original-to-expanded reverse-KL OPD restores cooperation, SAPO unlocks capacity, and expanded-to-original ExOPD with reward scale 1.25 transfers it back. Tables 1–2 report up to 22.2 domain-average percentage points over the original and 6.5 over same-backbone RL; evaluations average ten samples per problem and three training seeds. The 8/16/32/48-hour per-domain budgets on 16 H20 GPUs include all MoEvolve phases and match the compared methods’ wall-clock allowances. Router/expert and transfer-objective ablations support the mechanism. The original LG October19 new-submission batch plus official Sunday20EDT schedule supports inferred first paper availability October19T00Z; original October16T09:23:22Z receipt is retained. Actual full-source discovery occurred during this delayed backfill run, not on the report date. No author code or trained-checkpoint release was verified.
evidence.limitations: This requires additional training, larger intermediate active compute, valid reward functions and token-probability access; it is not training-free or reward-free. Equal wall-clock time on this fixed hardware is not equal FLOPs or a universal cost comparison. Separate domain-specific checkpoints do not establish one model simultaneously improving all domains. Tested backbones are at most30B total parameters; this does not establish trillion-parameter scaling or robustness outside the selected tasks. Maximum-expert expansion, ExOPD and checkpoint selection are additional recipe choices. V2 received October20 is not used for this October19 record; no independent reproduction.

entries.title: Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization
summary: Self-HPO alternates failure-guided harness revisions with reinforcement learning of the coding policy, using the updated policy and its unsolved training tasks to guide the next search round.

With Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, average resolve rate across three SWE benchmarks rises from 57.8% to 64.8%, offering a practical recipe for improving the model and its execution scaffold together rather than optimizing either component in isolation.

evidence.rationale: Full Sections 2–3, Table 1–3 and relevant Appendices A–E inspected. Two rounds alternate six harness candidates with 50 GRPO/BAR updates on 2,484 Python engineering training tasks. The self-proposer sees training failures and reference fixes but must not inject reference patches into solving context. Main evaluation averages three runs on 500 SWE-Verified,300 SWE-Multilingual and642 public V2 SWE-Pro tasks. Self-HPO scores 69.5/59.7/65.2 versus 61.0/54.2/58.3 for Base and 67.5/56.3/61.8 for matched policy-only RLVR. Cross-combinations retain some gains separately, with the final pair 69.5 exceeding 64.5 from evolved harness/base policy and 64.4 from seed harness/final policy. Original cs.CL October 19 batch plus official Eastern announcement schedule supports inferred paper availability2026-10-19T00:00Z; October 16 receipt is preserved. GitHub initial content commitOctober 19 at 01:39Z and HF model sole initial-release commitOctober 19 at 01:41Z corroborate the same window; earlier empty destination creation dates do not establish an earlier method release.
evidence.limitations: Only one backbone and coding domain; harness and policy receive different optimization operations, so the comparison does not establish universal compute-normalized superiority. Training uses executable reference outcomes and proposer-accessible training fixes, and policy training required eight B200 GPUs. Three-run means do not prove general deployment reliability; no independent reproduction. External-proposer HPO 71.6 is a separate Opus 4.8 setting and is not attributed to Self-HPO.

entries.title: MS-Eval: Benchmarking Sub-Agent Delegation and Orchestration in MCP-Intensive Working Scenarios
summary: MS-Eval pairs 166 tool-intensive work tasks with annotated delegation plans and a controlled harness, evaluating when subagents help as well as their success, critical-path steps and API-token cost.

Its eight-model study shows that specialization and context offloading can help, while unnecessary delegation often adds cost; this gives agent builders a more informative comparison than assuming that adding subagents improves every model.

evidence.rationale: Full Sections 3–7, Table 1 and relevant Appendices A–D inspected. Tasks span eight Toolathlon-Gym scenarios, with 89 annotated as delegation-needed and 77 not-needed; four delegation variants share a Kimi-Code scaffold. A 166-task comparison evaluates eight models, while the variant comparison uses DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731. Specialized roles score MSQ 20.8 versus 11.6 for general roles and 17.6 for plan-first in that setup. Critical steps count each parallel wave by its slowest subagent, not measured wall time; API billing is a fixed-price estimate. The full-benchmark Kimi-K3 Spec result improves success 10.2 percentage points at 0.4 USD lower mean token cost per task, whereas tested closed models incur higher cost with lower success. Original cs.AI October 19 batch and official schedule support inferred paper availability2026-10-19T00:00Z, separate from October 16 receipt. The announced author repository was checked by HTML and API and returns 404; it is omitted from publication.links.
evidence.limitations: One simulated tool environment and one harness; role prompts change the main agent even when it delegates nothing, and 305 of 625 categorized beneficial cases are main-agent-only. Delegation priors reflect the authors' parallelism/context-offloading assumptions; matching uses an LLM tagger and the custom MSQ weighting is not a universal quality score. Resource utilities condition on selected/successful subsets, and efficiency is critical steps rather than latency. No author implementation or independent reproduction verified.

entries.title: BaGuaLu-2: Taming Dynamic Memory Fluctuation for Efficient MoE Model Training over 10,000 GPUs
summary: BaGuaLu-2 adjusts activation-memory budgets for each pipeline microbatch and combines recomputation, offloading and reduced-precision storage when mixture-of-experts routing creates temporary load spikes.
Its detailed paper explains how a cost model and interleaved execution of neighboring batches can absorb those spikes without restarting training, improving utilization of large training clusters.

evidence.rationale: Read full SectionsI-VIII, Algorithms1-2 and evaluationVI, including the dependency conditions of fused dual-batch scheduling. Per-operator time/memory curves guide pipeline-phase budgets and a greedy conflict-checked mitigation selector; a compacted/cached dynamic program overlaps forward, backward, prior-batch offload and next-batch recovery. All evaluated pipeline degrees are at least4. On128-12,288 unnamed vendor GPUs (480TFLOP/s BF16,64GB HBM each;8/node,400GB/s intranode,4x400Gb/s internode), authors report mean throughput gains1.14x over Megatron-Kuai and1.13x over AdaPipe, with2.012EFLOP/s and about35%MFU for a1040B-parameter MoE at12,288GPUs. Baselines use the same initial parallelism and are adapted from dense-model systems. Paper receipt October16 07:40:24Z is preserved; the new full paper is in the original cs.DC Monday19 batch, whose release is inferred as October19T00Z from the official Sunday20Eastern schedule. The prior SC26 program already carried the broad mechanism and headline numbers; this entry selects the new inspectable full analysis, algorithms, configuration accounting and ablations, not a first announcement of those claims.
evidence.limitations: Throughput includes baseline OOM/restart warmup overhead but excludes human diagnosis time; it is not a restart-free kernel-speed comparison. Baselines are modified: only AdaPipe recomputation is enabled, and Megatron-Kuai receives MoE memory terms. The fused scheduling independence argument requires pipeline degree greater than2 and corresponding barriers; it is not a generic arbitrary-pipeline guarantee. Model configurations are GLM-derived and hardware-co-designed, not unmodified public checkpoints. Quantized activation storage is one allowed mitigation; no long-run convergence/quality study or public BaGuaLu-2 implementation was verified. Hardware vendor is not identified and no independent reproduction was performed.

entries.update_note: 2026-10-19: The detailed arXiv paper adds explicit activation-cost modeling, pipeline-aware budgets, conflict checks, a dependency-scoped dual-batch schedule, baseline/restart accounting and robustness ablations beyond the earlier official SC26 program abstract (https://arxiv.org/html/2610.23064v1; https://sc26.conference-program.com/presentation/?id=pap287&sess=sess211). The paper announcement is inferred from the original cs.DC Monday19 batch and official release schedule (https://arxiv.org/list/cs.DC/recent?skip=0&show=2000; https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html); the conference abstract has no verified exact first-public timestamp, so no earliest-work availability timestamp is asserted. This is a new detailed-paper review, not a new-code claim.

entries.title: No Single Tokenizer Feature Reliably Predicts Downstream Language Model Performance
summary: Across three small-model suites and nine languages, this study finds that popular tokenizer metrics correlate inconsistently with downstream quality, even when individual task correlations appear strong.
The results support validating tokenizer choices on representative tasks and languages instead of treating compression or a single intrinsic score as a reliable accuracy proxy.

evidence.rationale: Full Sections 3–10 and the model, evaluation, statistical and robustness appendices inspected again. Three suites cover 14 TokSuite 1B models, 45 usable TIMTC 350M models after nine OOV exclusions, and multilingual VISTA 130M/350M models; 29 intrinsic metrics and 48 distinct benchmark tasks span nine languages. The analysis z-scores accuracy within language and task, corrects multiple comparisons, controls parameter counts and repeats the analysis after excluding near-chance cases. The strongest aggregate correlations are only r=0.27, 0.24 and 0.22, while signs and rankings change across tasks, languages and suites. A metric explains at most an additional 0.021 R-squared beyond model size; pairs of intrinsic metrics reach at most 0.09 joint R-squared. Existing VISTA training code and model collections were verified both in the prior run and today. This was a reviewed but unpublished reserve on October 17, below that run’s selected contributions; fresh reassessment now includes its useful tokenizer-selection lesson within the remaining 72-hour lookback. Its original October 17 first-seen time is preserved. No indexing delay is claimed.
evidence.limitations: These observational correlations do not show that tokenizers do not matter or that a better metric cannot exist. Models are at most 1B parameters, some tasks are near chance, language coverage and suite training budgets differ, vocabulary sizes change embedding parameter counts, and annotated intrinsic resources are uneven across languages. Compression can still reduce cost without predicting accuracy. The VISTA link is training code, not the complete current paper-analysis pipeline. The main analysis repository, unavailable with 404 responses during the prior run, loaded today, but its sole observed code commit is October 18 at 21:13Z, after the report’s 10:00Z cutoff. That later artifact is not used as an in-window contribution or advertised as available by the cutoff; its exact first public visibility is not inferred from Git metadata. An undated author homepage lists the title without a paper link and does not establish an earlier full-method release.

entries.title: Training Reasoning Models to Generate Diverse Scientific Ideas
summary: After supervised warm-starting, this recipe trains an 8B model to generate three scientific ideas in one rollout and rewards each idea’s judged quality multiplied by its difference from earlier ideas.

The resulting sets outperform quality-only RL on the authors’ document-grounded benchmark, suggesting a practical way to discourage duplicate proposals while leaving scientific validity and source grounding as separate checks.

evidence.rationale: Full primary HTML, including the reward, training, judging, human-study and execution appendices, inspected. Sections 2–6, Equations 2 and 7, Tables 1, 3, 4 and 11, and Appendices B–F describe one K=3 rollout, a shared GRPO set advantage, a quality-times-nearest-prior-distance reward, schema gating and a capped length penalty. SFT and RL use 7,172 English NLP training instances; the main test has 1,740 instances across 16 scientific domains. In Table 1, the Qwen3-8B no-thinking model reaches judged Creative Utility 0.64 versus 0.21 after SFT and 0.38 with impact-only RL; idea distance is 0.88 versus 0.38 for impact-only RL. Grounding falls from 0.90 after no-thinking SFT to 0.61 after RL; the thinking variant trades lower utility (0.51) for higher grounding (0.81). The four-expert, 60-instance human pilot reports 2.17 promising ideas per set versus Claude’s 2.20. Appendix F’s execution pilot has 15 source instances (14 for the thinking variant), using a budgeted coding agent and its own experimental verdicts, not independently validated scientific discoveries. The author-linked repository currently contains only a coming-soon README. First inspected during this run; the paper is an unreported October 16 new-submission batch contribution inside the 72-hour lookback, so it is a delayed discovery rather than an October 18 release. Original October 15 receipt date is retained.
evidence.limitations: All results are author-reported. LLM judges define quality, distance, grounding and most benchmark outcomes; a 2026 test-year split alone does not prove absence of training contamination. The within-set reward does not ensure diversity across the population: IdeaSeed method-type entropy is 0.65 for no-thinking and 0.73 for thinking, below the reported human 0.87. The DARLING comparison also changes initialization, rollout grouping and clipping, so it does not isolate only where diversity is rewarded; the impact-only ablation is the cleaner comparison. Four experts and 15 execution instances are small pilots, and the execution agent’s self-reported support/refutation is not verified discovery. Training uses an external distance-judge API in addition to the local H200 allocation. Code, data and models are promised, not released in the verified project. No broad scientific-discovery or universal SoTA claim is supported.

entries.title: GraphACM: Graph-based Action Consistency Measurement for Uncertainty Quantification in LLM Agents
summary: GraphACM aligns repeated agent runs into a shared state-action graph and measures whether they choose the same actions in comparable decision contexts.

This training-free signal localizes behavioral disagreement and distinguishes more reliably solved tasks in the tested environments, helping builders assess execution stability without treating consistency as a correctness guarantee.

evidence.rationale: Sections 2-3, Tables 1-2 and Appendices A-D inspected using the full HTML and complete 13-page PDF. Ten temperature-1 rollouts per task/model pair cover 134 ALFWorld, 168 AppWorld and 200 WebShop tasks with Qwen3.8-27B, Gemma-4-31B-IT and GPT-5.4-mini. State-conditioned action agreement, visitor weighting and action-count normalization yield mean success-discrimination AUROC 0.811 versus 0.769 for verbalized confidence and 0.729 for the best consistency comparator. Success labels require at least 5/10 successful runs. Delayed editorial catch-up from the October 16 original cs.AI batch, already visible in our archived October 17 listing; this is not a late-indexing claim or an October 18 release. The archived retrieval timestamp is retained as first_seen_at, and full verification was completed October 18. Availability at 2026-10-16T00:00Z is inferred from the dated batch and official announcement schedule.
evidence.limitations: Uses ten repeated executions and benchmark-specific state/history abstractions; prospective single-execution deployment and calibrated failure probabilities are not established. The label and score derive from the same rollout set. Consistently wrong WebShop behavior remains possible and results there are weaker. No dedicated author implementation or earlier primary release was verified, and no independent reproduction was performed.

entries.title: AgentPerturb: Evaluating LLM Agent Robustness under Controlled Interaction Perturbations
summary: AgentPerturb builds matched clean and noisy agent tasks by varying user requests, procedures, inherited context and tool contracts across missing, distracting and incorrect information.
Its two-environment study exposes different failure patterns and costly recovery tails, providing a practical test design for robustness that clean benchmark scores can miss.

evidence.rationale: Methods, results, limitations and relevant Appendices A/B/E/F.6 inspected. The pipeline creates 12 one-target perturbation families and checks goal preservation, a viable recovery path and executability with an LLM verifier plus native validators; missing information can add a clarification step. Each of ten models runs 25 clean and 300 perturbed episodes per benchmark under a common Codex CLI scaffold. Table 1 model-averaged APEX partial-credit scores fall 70.3 to 55.0, while Toolathlon binary success falls 25.0% to 18.4%; these are different metrics. A focused Hunyuan-3-High analysis reports 73% higher mean tokens per successful perturbed trajectory with little median change. Delayed editorial catch-up from the October 16 original cs.AI batch, already visible in our archived October 17 listing; this is not a late-indexing claim or an October 18 release. The archived retrieval timestamp is retained as first_seen_at, and full verification was completed October 18. Availability at 2026-10-16T00:00Z is inferred from the dated batch and official announcement schedule.
evidence.limitations: Only 25 tasks per benchmark; Toolathlon is a completion-selected 25/79 subset, not a random full-benchmark sample, and unscored runs are excluded. One trajectory per condition and provider-dependent decoding limit generalization; fine-grained family comparisons use only five models. The semantic-verifier gate has no measured human agreement or error rate. The linked GitHub repository is empty at verification, so code/data release and independent matched-edit audit are not established. No independent reproduction.

entries.title: LCT: Losslessly Compressed Tensors with GPU friendly execution for Training
summary: LCT stores BF16 weights, saved activations and optimizer buffers in a lossless exponent-coded format, using parallel GPU encoding, fused updates and a shared overflow arena for repeated compression during training.

The new paper quantifies a memory-versus-step-time trade-off and explains how the format adapts to changing tensor magnitudes, enabling longer tested sequences on a memory-constrained GPU without quantizing the stored BF16 values.

evidence.rationale: Read methodology4.1-4.7, storage/scale analysis5, experiments6 and relevant AppendicesA-C, including timing/memory accounting and training integration. Bounded Huffman prefixes plus literal escapes compress exponents while preserving sign/fraction bytes; dense matrix products still require reconstruction. On one RTX3090 with PyTorch2.14/Triton3.8, activation compression in162M NanoGPT cuts peak allocated memory16058to12103MiB(24.6%) while optimizer-step time rises8.411to9.013s(7.2%). All-component compression yields11964.6MiB/9.136s, and a3400-step run has similar validation loss. Qwen3-4B-Base full-parameter BF16/Muon memory-time tests at batch1 fit3500tested tokens versus1000for the baseline; at1000, memory is21327.8to16262.4MiB with4.006to4.273s step time. This is a new detailed paper/analysis of older public code, not a new implementation release. The prior README says paper-coming-soon; the complete October12 tree contains only a graphical-abstractPDF, not the paper.
evidence.limitations: Storage is lossless for input BF16 bit patterns; converting FP32 to BF16 first still loses information, and this does not prove bitwise-identical whole training. Compression depends on exponent statistics, block padding and overflow; small or mismatched tensors can expand. Requires explicit custom-autograd/operator integration, and compressed weights are not ordinary registered nn.Parameters. Shared-arena sizing must include live replacements/fragmentation. Training time/peak memory use only five measured optimizer steps after three warmups; Qwen tests do not establish long-run fine-tuning quality. Reported memory is PyTorch allocated, not allocator-reserved or all device memory; training includes the entire shared arena. Only BF16 is supported here and GEMMs decode first. Code was inspected but not executed; no independent reproduction.

entries.update_note: 2026-10-16: The newly announced detailed paper adds bounded-code/scale-shift/storage analysis and controlled codec, NanoGPT and Qwen memory-time evaluations to the earlier public LCT implementation (https://arxiv.org/html/2610.22179v1; https://arxiv.org/list/cs.LG/recent?skip=0&show=2000; https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html). The repository was created October4 with code commits through October12; its README still marks the paper coming soon and its inspected pre-window tree has no paperPDF (https://github.com/Maxzhu123/Losslessly_Compressed_Tensors; https://api.github.com/repos/Maxzhu123/Losslessly_Compressed_Tensors/git/trees/396b9d6fb725956cb0735a83b5de368319d0b823?recursive=1). Commit dates document earlier content, not exact first-public visibility. Preserve October15 as this paper's receipt date; the paper update is inferred as October16T00Z from its original cs.LG batch and official schedule. This is delayed editorial review within the72-hour window, not a claim of newly released code.

entries.title: Coordination-Free Workload Regularization for Variable-Cost Distributed Training
summary: Batch Cost Lookahead buffers a bounded window inside each training worker and regroups it into equal-record-count batches with similar estimated cost, without exchanging sample metadata across workers.

This reduces synchronization waiting for variable-length training while retaining the existing batch-count interface, with explicit diagnostics for oversized records and persistent imbalance that local scheduling cannot fix.

evidence.rationale: Editorial catch-up of an October16 arXiv announcement already screened as a reserve on October17; this is delayed selection, not an indexing-delay claim. Read Sections1-10, Algorithm1 and all evaluation tables. The fixed-cardinality contract conserves each window's records and uses classical longest-processing-time initialization plus bounded heavy/light swaps. On Llama3.2-1B NeMo-RL0.7.0 SFT with FSDP2/BF16/FA3 on eight H200 GPUs, lookahead32 versus1 in the same per-rank pipeline improves mean wall-clock step speed by0.4-30.5% across11 corpora, over three300-step repeats excluding20warmups. All arms use the same per-corpus p99 cap. The abstract's5.0-16.7% comparison against pooledMFFD includes input-path differences and is cross-campaign. Paper receipt is October15 03:22:50Z; public availability is inferred from the original cs.DC Friday16 batch and official Thursday20:00Eastern schedule.
evidence.limitations: The assignment heuristic is classical; the contribution is its bounded streaming deployment contract and measured boundary analysis, not a new global optimizer. Length-cost simulation is not GPU speedup. Two matched no-lookahead arms were not rerun after prior OOMs. The larger1.197-1.343x result uses an internal sequential recommender and weak scaling from8to32H200 ranks, not LLM scaling evidence. Local reordering cannot resolve a dominant infeasible record or different total cost across rank shards. It changes optimizer-step sample grouping; p99 truncation quality, held-out SFT quality and exact midstream restart are untested. No dedicated public implementation was verified; no independent reproduction.

entries.title: Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins
summary: Anthropic documents an LLM-assisted investigation that tested pseudorandom-generator hypotheses and recovered the origins of several standardized elliptic-curve seeds and base points.
Its published verification code makes this a useful case study of combining model-generated hypotheses with exact computational checks in scientific investigation.

evidence.rationale: The October 16 primary report explains generator scanning, hidden-state recovery, backward reconstruction and timestamp checks, and includes code and expected outputs for ten prime-curve seeds, four binary-curve seeds and six base points. Its stated sub-half-hour discovery is author-reported.
evidence.limitations: A single investigation with an internal research model, not a controlled comparison or reusable agent-system evaluation. B-163 and several base-point origins remain unexplained; skipped candidate curves leave historical selection criteria uncertain. The result does not break ECDSA or demonstrate a weakness in the standardized curves. No independent reproduction.

entries.title: SGLang Powers Beam in Production
summary: SGLang integrates Beam's hybrid sliding-window and full-attention mixture-of-experts model with fused precision-sensitive operations and a jointly budgeted target-and-drafter cache for blockwise speculative decoding.

The report explains how cache reuse, draft-memory placement and supported parallel layouts fit together for long-context agents, with public serving recipes and replay scripts that separate simulated acceptance from natural-workload measurements.

evidence.rationale: Read the full October 16 report, including target/draft cache placement, DFlash2 with attention data parallelism, heterogeneous TP transfer, precision/fusion gates and the reproduction appendix. The public benchmark branch, serving cookbook and PRs 40331/40492/40909 were retrieved. Beam has 501B total/23B active parameters, hybrid attention, FP32 routing and rounded scaled residuals. On four GB300 GPUs, the OpenHands NVFP4 TP4 replay uses 13 turns, about 74K initial tokens, about 220 output tokens per turn and approximately 92% prefix-cache hits; its 127.6K total token/s/GPU headline at concurrency 32 uses fixed simulated acceptance length four. The separate AgentX replay reports 83,504 total token/s/GPU and 43.9 P90 token/s/user at concurrency 96. These are distinct workloads, not an engine leaderboard.
evidence.limitations: Total throughput includes cached input tokens and is not newly computed or output-token throughput. OpenHands uses simulated acceptance with real draft tokens, so it does not measure natural acceptance or model accuracy; AgentX has a different workload and latency percentile. Shared draft placement excludes HiCache, host retraction and DCP; private fallbacks and startup gates apply, and draft capture requires PP=1. BF16 and dynamic FP8 do not use the NVFP4 MegaMoE extension. TPU recipes are forthcoming. Production-API use is author-reported rather than independent reliability evidence. Miles training results are separate from serving quality, and no author code or model experiment was executed.

entries.title: Hyper Optimizing Kimi K3 in vLLM: Moving Fast and Responsibly
summary: This vLLM engineering report replaces Kimi K3's decode path with workload-tuned kernels that fuse projections, residual operations and GPU communication while overlapping expert computation and weight prefetch.

It pairs measured decode gains with a scoped validation process for agent-written optimizations, showing how to accelerate supported Blackwell configurations without treating one synthetic benchmark as a general serving result.

evidence.rationale: Read the complete dated Markdown and PR 61867 description, covering CuTe DSL projection/KDA kernels, DCP, NVLink fusion, sharded router work, expert overlap and weight prefetching. The blog reports no-speculation aggregate TP-group gains of 1.31-1.92x across TP8/16 and batch sizes 1-64 on GB300. Its 842 versus 488 decode token/s comparison uses synthetic DSpark acceptance length six and excludes prefill. The merged opt-in implementation includes task/numerical checks and investigation of a compiler load-before-wait bug. The contribution selected is the new detailed engineering report and validation evidence, not a first-ever code release: the PR opened October 15. The displayed blog date is October 16; its source was added October 17 01:21 UTC, which is source provenance rather than an asserted exact website publication time. Delayed discovery: the optimization work, scoped benchmarks and validation were already described in the October 15 PR, within this report's 72-hour discovery lookback and before its main window. This entry inspects the October 16 detailed blog on October 17; it does not claim the method or code first appeared in the main coverage window.
evidence.limitations: Scope is GB300 TP8/TP16 within one NVLink domain; speculative batch coverage is narrower than the no-speculation batch-64 range. Synthetic acceptance and decode-only throughput do not establish normal serving speed. The AgentX 1.8x interactivity comparison uses 16 optimized GPUs versus eight earlier GPUs. Blog and PR use different benchmark snapshots. Task scores near one standard error and sensitive long-context checks are not bitwise equivalence or general production reliability proofs. Development and review savings are not quantified. No independent reproduction was performed. The PR predates the main window, so the dated blog does not reset the optimization's age; inclusion is explicitly a delayed discovery, not an indexing-delay claim.

entries.title: Priming Base Models for Agentic Post-Training: An Open Midtraining Recipe
summary: This documented midtraining recipe combines natural software-engineering data with a bounded share of agent traces at 256K context before supervised post-training.

Matched post-training comparisons on two Nemotron model sizes show stronger coding-agent results in several settings, while the data and masking ablations provide concrete guidance for building and evaluating this intermediate training stage.

evidence.rationale: The complete main text and Appendices A-E were inspected. The token blend contains 40.8% issue-PR data, 20% dependency-packed repositories, 10% agent traces, 3% diffs, 1.2% build/CI logs, 20% pretraining replay and 5% long-context data; trace tool responses are masked and only assistant turns contribute loss. Nemotron 3.5 Lightning (30B total/3B active) receives up to 500B midtraining tokens and Super (120B/12B) receives 280B, followed by identical 33B-token short or 100B-token full SFT. Table 3 reports Lightning full-SFT success changing from 60.7 to 64.5 on SWE-bench Verified, 55.8 to 62.8 Multilingual, and 32.0 to 35.5 Pro; Table 6 reports Super DeepSWE 11.7 to 15.7 and SWE-bench Verified 72.9 to 74.3. SWE-bench Verified uses 500 tasks and three rollouts per task; DeepSWE pass@1 is averaged over four runs. Public availability is inferred as October 16 00:00 UTC from the verified cs.CL new-submission batch and official schedule, retaining the original October 15 14:58:21 UTC receipt date.
evidence.limitations: Added midtraining compute is not compared with spending the same tokens on longer pretraining or SFT. Comparisons use one run each, only Nemotron models and agentic-focused post-training; Super full-SFT Multilingual falls from 69.0 to 67.9 and Pro from 53.9 to 51.8. The single-seed, 20-step RL pilot shows only that an SFT advantage survives the start of RL, not better eventual RL trainability. Some one- or two-point differences fall within reported run variation. Data-processing scripts and metadata are promised for a future version, so this is a documented recipe rather than a verified complete training-corpus or implementation release.

entries.title: Does On-Policy Distillation Need to Complete Every Rollout?
summary: STOPD randomly truncates student rollouts at block boundaries and reweights retained token losses to preserve the expected full-rollout gradient sum.

Across tested Qwen students and mathematics, coding and instruction-following tasks, the authors report similar accuracy with 25-48% fewer generated tokens and 1.3-2.2x faster training steps, offering a practical way to reduce distillation cost.

evidence.rationale: Sections 3-5 and relevant Appendices A/B/D-H were inspected. STOPD samples independent cutoffs, rounds each to a block end, and uses exact inverse inclusion probabilities with K=128 after 25 Vanilla warmup steps. The main comparison distills Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 into Qwen3-1.7B-Base over 250 steps, three training seeds and batch 256 on two H100s: reported full-step times are 941 to 513 seconds for math, 566 to 260 for code, and 104 to 80 for instruction following, including generation, teacher scoring, updates and other overhead. Vanilla versus STOPD endpoint aggregate accuracy is 30.1 versus 29.4 for math, 28.5 versus 28.1 for code, and 59.8 versus 60.1 for instruction following. Additional 30B-A3B-teacher experiments use 4B/8B students on two H200/GB200 GPUs respectively. Public availability is inferred as October 16 00:00 UTC from the verified cs.LG new-submission batch and official schedule; the original October 15 06:22:08 UTC receipt date is retained.
evidence.limitations: The expected unnormalized gradient and token-count sums are preserved only under budget-invariant generation, prefix-local loss, independent truncation and exact inclusion probabilities. The actual normalized loss uses the previous batch token-count estimate and can retain a scale mismatch; optimizer bounds compare one step from identical parameters and state, not complete training trajectories. Evidence covers Qwen 1.7B-8B students and 250-step runs, with speed depending on rollout length, hardware and scheduling. The weight-free random-truncation ablation also preserves accuracy closely, while inverse weighting better aligns response lengths, so accuracy alone does not prove the weights necessary. No author implementation or model artifact URL was verified; cited Muon code is not a STOPD release.

entries.title: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models
summary: This framework evolves Python circuit generators with parallel algorithm families, a diverse program archive, and an independent evaluator that checks correctness before scoring quantum resource costs.
It provides a concrete example of evaluator-guided agents discovering new algorithmic structures, rather than only refining a fixed implementation.

evidence.rationale: Methods, Figure 1 and Table 1 describe fresh agent sessions, MAP-Elites retention and eight task-specific evaluations. The Reed–Solomon decoder uses about 440,000 Toffolis and 1,837 qubits versus 5.1 million and 1,938 for its reconstructed baseline. Author circuits, evaluators and Lean proofs are available.
evidence.limitations: These are simulated logical resource counts, not hardware runtime or a general agent leaderboard. Some tasks permit distribution-specific failures; sampled validation is not a universal proof. The Hermitian comparator is a naive construction, not a prior published reversible circuit. No independent reproduction.

entries.title: Mosaic: Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Mosaic trains agents across context-compaction and subagent sessions by combining outcome-aware session-use guidance with a per-session signal based on changes in correct-answer likelihood.
This assigns more specific feedback to useful state transfers, improving BrowseComp success while reducing average session counts in the tested 4B agent.

evidence.rationale: Methods 3.1–3.2, Table 1 and Appendices C–D specify critic-free shaping, type-wise normalization and matched training. With Qwen3.5-4B, compaction accuracy rises 35.31→38.86% while sessions fall 3.17→2.35; forking rises 31.44→32.46% with 4.43→3.77 sessions. Training uses 1,000 REDSearcher tasks; BrowseComp evaluation covers 1,266 questions. ArXiv availability is inferred from its original dated batch and official schedule.
evidence.limitations: One backbone and benchmark; session count is a proxy rather than measured end-to-end cost. Correct answers are needed for training-time likelihood scoring, and immediate gains approximate branching-session contributions. Production asynchrony is untested. The project was retrieved, but no released implementation was verified. No independent reproduction.

entries.title: LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents
summary: LEASH uses a small computer-use model's hidden-state similarity to past successes and failures to decide when to hand a task to a stronger model and when to request reassessment after handoff.
It offers a way to allocate expensive model calls dynamically, with near always-strong success at lower estimated inference cost in the authors' OSWorld evaluation.

evidence.rationale: Sections 3–4 and Appendices A–B define reference-bank calibration, gates and oversight. On 262 held-out OSWorld tasks, the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B configuration reaches 73.66% success at $0.4117/task versus 72.90% and $0.5094 for always-on Opus 5; costs include Manager and monitoring calls. ArXiv availability is inferred from the dated batch and official schedule.
evidence.limitations: One benchmark and token-priced reference costs, not measured hardware cost or latency. Reference trajectories require upfront collection; failure risk need not predict escalation benefit. Shadow monitoring faces distribution shift and its causal effect is not isolated. No independent reproduction.

entries.title: ETH: Data-Balanced Heterogeneous Pipeline Parallelism for Training Large Models
summary: ETH balances heterogeneous training pipelines by assigning different local batch sizes as well as different layer and parallelism layouts, avoiding the coarse memory trade-offs of layer balancing alone.

Its hierarchical search and block-wise gradient synchronization make a larger configuration space practical, with reported iteration-time improvements on mixed Ascend devices and A100/RTX3090 clusters.

evidence.rationale: Reviewed the HPP formulation, greedy local-batch allocation and stage refinement, block-wise AllReduce, cached/pruned search, implementation, Sections 7-8 and appendices. Main tests use GPT-3 350M-175B and LLaMA-2 70B on mixed Ascend 910B2/B3/B4 devices, chiefly at sequence length 2,048 and global batch 1,024. NVIDIA tests cover 350M-13B on A100/RTX 3090 clusters with 100 Gbps links. Main Ascend iteration speedups are 1.36-2.00x over HexiScale and 1.20-1.84x over Metis; a 2,000-iteration Enwiki check reports approximately 0.1% loss differences. Public code predates the paper: the July 29 initial tree has no PDF, and the October 16 change only adds a citation. Selection covers the new detailed paper/evidence. Public-paper timing is inferred from the primary cs.DC October 16 batch and official schedule, preserving the October 15 receipt.
evidence.limitations: Search is heuristic and approximate pruning can discard better candidates, so no global optimum is guaranteed. The cost model assumes 1F1B with pipeline, tensor and data parallelism; context and expert parallelism are not included. Benefits depend on batch size, hardware imbalance and profiling, and HPP adds communication. NVIDIA validation stops at 13B while larger-model results use Ascend. Loss similarity on one corpus does not prove broad downstream equivalence. Abstract headline search speedups are avoided in favor of scoped body results. Public code was inspected but not executed; there is no independent reproduction.

entries.update_note: 2026-10-16: The newly announced paper supplies the formal heterogeneous-pipeline/batch-allocation method, block-wise synchronization, search design and detailed Ascend/NVIDIA evaluation beyond the older implementation (https://arxiv.org/html/2610.22035v1; https://arxiv.org/list/cs.DC/recent?skip=0&show=2000; https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html; https://github.com/YuMJie/ETH). The initial July 29 code tree contains no paper PDF; commit dates are provenance, not proof of an exact first-public timestamp. The preserved October 15 published_on is this paper's receipt date.

entries.title: ReFlow: Replay-Driven Decoupling for Efficient RL Post-Training
summary: ReFlow mixes a bounded, down-weighted share of recently used trajectories into asynchronous reinforcement-learning batches, reducing the trainer's dependence on expensive fresh rollouts.

Prewarmed workers and an adaptive scheduler move GPUs between generation and training as demand changes, increasing processed-training-token throughput while preserving comparable training-reward progress in the tested reasoning and agent workloads.

evidence.rationale: Reviewed Sections 1-8, the replay-weighting analysis, worker transitions, both schedulers and complete evaluations. The VeRL/Ray/vLLM/FSDP2 system tests Qwen3-4B/8B/14B/32B on 8-128 H800 GPUs using DAPO math, APPS coding and ReTool sandbox reasoning. Replay fraction and replay loss weight are capped/set at 0.5, with maximum policy lag one; sampling is random and reinsertion unfiltered. Authors report up to 2.06x trainer-processed token throughput, reward-versus-step/time curves, and 5.72/9.20 s resource rebalances on 32 GPUs. Public-paper timing is inferred from the PRIMARY cs.LG October 16 batch and official release schedule, rather than the October 15 receipt timestamp.
evidence.limitations: Throughput includes replayed tokens consumed by the trainer; it is not fresh-trajectory generation throughput. Quality evidence is training reward rather than held-out reasoning or coding evaluation. Throughput windows are five measured steps after five warmups, or ten after ten for coding. The local gradient-error argument assumes unbiased unused samples, bounded replay bias and uncorrelated centered errors; it is not a global convergence guarantee. Prewarmed hybrid workers require CPU offload and compatible replica groups, and adaptation depends on workload. The code is awaiting approval and not yet released. No independent reproduction was performed.

entries.title: When the KV Cache Is Slower Than the GPU: Scaling Remote KV Tiers for Context-Parallel Prefill
summary: This study explains why a remote key-value cache can be slower than recomputing a prompt, then shards cache work across context-parallel ranks and remote servers while moving loads off the engine's blocking path.
Its production-trace replay and bandwidth-plus-fixed-cost model give serving engineers a practical way to decide when cache reuse helps, and to separate capacity benefits from first-token latency.

evidence.rationale: Reviewed Sections 3-8, all tables, the collective-safe sharding protocol and the linked LMCache PR. GLM-5.3 FP8 runs on one 8-GPU B300 PCP8/EP8 prefill engine using vLLM 0.31.0 and LMCache 0.5.5. A 683-request production trace and a primed 450-request subset support the cost model; on the hit-heavy subset, final prefill-leg p99 is 0.67 s versus 83.32 s for the overloaded single-server baseline, with 98.5% of prompt tokens cached. Final remote-hit median remains 0.40 s versus 0.31 s for recomputation. This is a new detailed paper and evaluation of engineering whose sharding PR opened October 8. Public-paper availability is inferred as October 16 00:00 UTC from its primary cs.DC batch and the official announcement schedule; the October 15 receipt date is preserved. The linked PR 5545 implements the synchronous sharding component, not all asynchronous extensions or client fixes evaluated in the paper.
evidence.limitations: Each condition ran once; differences below about 10% are not established. The dramatic p99 ratio repairs an overloaded hit-heavy queue rather than showing a universal cache speedup. Replays omit decode handoff and shared multi-engine contention, and the selected subset fits the private cache. The approximately 17K-token crossover is a one-point-fitted prediction, not a measured general threshold. Deployment comparisons change parallelism and placement too. Correctness evidence is needle retrieval and soak testing, not bit-exact or broad answer-quality proof. The linked PR remains open; no independent reproduction was performed. PR 5545 explicitly rejects asynchronous loading; the paper references separate extensions and fixes, so this link is not a complete reproduction artifact.

entries.update_note: 2026-10-16: The newly announced paper adds a detailed fixed-cost/bandwidth model, collective-safe remote-cache protocol, production-trace evaluation and limitations beyond the earlier sharding implementation (https://arxiv.org/html/2610.21500v1; https://arxiv.org/list/cs.DC/recent?skip=0&show=2000; https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html; https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/5545). The PR opened October 8, which is provenance rather than an asserted exact first-public timestamp. The preserved October 15 published_on is this paper's receipt date, not the implementation's release date.

entries.title: The COUNT: Counting N-grams Unlocks Scaling on Host Memory and Training-Free Adaptation
summary: COUNT adds corpus-count memory during language-model pretraining by combining the model's output embeddings using read-only n-gram statistics stored in host RAM.

Models trained with COUNT can later adapt by swapping these tables without updating their weights, providing a way to improve language modeling and domain specialization through additional host memory.

evidence.rationale: October 15 public availability is inferred from the dated new-submission batch and official schedule. Sections 2–6 and Appendix A inspect 60M–1B backbones, 11 validation sources and 74 downstream configurations; fitted loss frontiers correspond to 46–89% more standard-transformer 6ND compute. Author code, tables and checkpoints are accessible.
evidence.limitations: Flagship tables require about 797 GB host RAM and summarize the full Dolma corpus; table construction and extra gather work are outside 6ND. Measured throughput is slightly lower, not faster. COUNT requires modified pretraining; domain accuracy gains are mixed, and released core code omits the optimized runtime used for throughput measurements. No independent reproduction.

entries.title: LatentLoop: Scaling Looped MoE Models with Asymmetric Compute Allocation
summary: LatentLoop's new release supplies three pretrained checkpoints and a native inference loader for its mixture-of-experts architecture, which compresses the first loop pass and retains a full-resolution second pass.

These artifacts let researchers test asymmetric compute allocation without repeating pretraining; the previously documented experiments match resource budgets and show lower validation loss across 15 settings.

evidence.rationale: The update is the October 15 checkpoint and loader release. Hugging Face records model-repository creation at 06:56:35 UTC and modification at 07:37 UTC; code history adds checkpoint support and native inference loading at 07:45 UTC, before cutoff. The model card lists 1.3B, 3B and 7B endpoints, configurations and checksums. The original 24-page project PDF already contained the methods, ablations and 15 matched settings.
evidence.limitations: Exact first public visibility of earlier code and project artifacts is unknown, so no earliest-public timestamp is assigned. Models use one FineWeb-Edu stream, 4K context and one training seed; compute savings are fitted theoretical FLOPs rather than guaranteed latency. Checkpoints omit optimizer and RNG state, and released code omits internal experiments and analysis. No independent reproduction.

entries.update_note: 2026-10-15: three largest-budget pretrained checkpoints (1.3B, 3B and 7B), model and tokenizer configurations, and native incremental inference loading are now available at https://huggingface.co/yhx12/LatentLoop and https://github.com/lcqysl/LatentLoop. The checked model metadata records creation at 06:56:35 UTC and modification at 07:37 UTC, while the 07:45 UTC code revision adds loader and checkpoint support. Earlier October 14 code and project history already includes the full paper and headline results; those results and the method are not claimed new. Git chronology does not establish exact first public visibility.

entries.title: More Methods, Better Agents? A Reality Check on Self-Distillation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: This study reruns ten self-distillation approaches against group-relative policy optimization across four text-agent benchmarks and three model sizes, comparing final scores, learning stability and measured training cost.

The released implementation and detailed evaluation protocol help researchers choose training baselines: gains depend on the setting, and additional teacher computation frequently fails to improve performance.

evidence.rationale: The 39-page primary PDF supplies 132 training runs, 100 updates per run and eight sampled final-evaluation rollout seeds on Qwen3.5-2B/4B/9B. Only PCSD and AgentOPSD exceed GRPO's equal-weight twelve-setting mean; 112 of 120 alternatives take longer to train. Tables S5/S13–S16 separate mixed task metrics, net training time and broader recorded GPU-hours; method adaptations are explicit.
evidence.limitations: Eight rollout seeds measure evaluation variation, not independent retraining variability. The study uses fixed validation/final task sets, method-specific hyperparameters/adaptations, a 100-step horizon, four simulated text environments and one model family. Its heterogeneous-score mean is descriptive, not universal ranking; timing is specific to eight H800 GPUs. No independent reproduction here.

entries.update_note: 2026-10-15: the complete paper adds executable method definitions, adaptation details, training records and cost accounting beyond the earlier project preview; the author implementation is now available. The project history includes an October 14 06:51 UTC preview with headline results, but commit time does not prove public visibility. This entry covers the detailed paper and released implementation, not a claim that its headline findings first appeared today; paper availability is inferred from the dated October 15 announcement batch and official schedule.

entries.title: Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting
summary: The authors periodically restart communicating research agents from their best candidate while clearing conversation and candidate histories, helping stalled searches explore larger changes.

Across four code-optimization and model-training tasks, four-agent teams with this reset policy outperform their tested single-agent and independent parallel baselines at matched model spend, suggesting a practical memory policy for prolonged automated discovery.

evidence.rationale: October 15 new-submission listing and official schedule imply 00:00 UTC paper availability; submission was October 14 at 17:49:37 UTC. Full 14-page PDF, Sections 3–5, Tables 1–4 and Appendix B inspected, including visual checks of Tables 1–3. Pi/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, three runs per configuration: AHC014 mean best score is 1, 103k versus 964k for independent parallel agents. A same-state 30-proposal ablation gives communicating teams +9.2% after reset versus +1.4% on continuation.
evidence.limitations: Four tasks and one model/harness; reset timing is fixed, not learned. Dollar budgets cover model spend rather than total experiment compute or elapsed time. Main comparisons combine communication and resetting; the same-state ablation better isolates resetting. No dedicated author implementation was verified, and results were not reproduced.

entries.title: The Wealth of Agents: Scaling Agentic AI Across Developers
summary: This study models independently developed agents as an ecosystem and combines specialized systems through task decomposition, learned routing and answer composition.

In a controlled simulation of developers, its specialist coalition reaches about 70% on the evaluated GAIA split while individual specialists reach at most 35%, illustrating how complementary capabilities can matter more than standalone scores.

evidence.rationale: Submitted October 14 at 17:19:11 UTC and listed as a new October 15 paper. Sections 3–7 and Appendices A.4/B/C inspected. The GAIA experiment constructs 54 specialists versus nine generalists with equal aggregate development iterations; half the validation set trains the router and half evaluates it. Figure 5 comparisons average four runs. A learned contextual router reaches 70.13%, versus 61.04% without router learning.
evidence.limitations: Developers are simulated by meta-agents, not independent real organizations, and evaluation covers two datasets. Coordination can increase cost and reduce accuracy on SealQA or generalist pools. Theory assumes stylized development costs, routing and additive capabilities, omits coordination cost, and does not establish convergence to specialization. Security, compensation and real ecosystem deployment remain open; no dedicated implementation was verified.

entries.title: Into the Unknown: Benchmarking AI agents on open scientific research problems
summary: Into the Unknown evaluates scientific agents on 15 researcher-proposed follow-up problems using explicit integrity, completeness and scientific-success rubrics tied to submitted code and logs.

In its expanded nine-agent evaluation, none of 135 submissions passes all strict gates and 114 fail integrity checks, providing a concrete testbed for separating credible research execution from persuasive paper writing.

evidence.rationale: New detailed paper is in the October 15 batch; submission was October 13 at 20:25:59 UTC. Main methods/results and Appendices A/B inspected in the 163-page PDF. The October 13 project history expands the evaluator from 342 to 540 judgments covering all 135 submissions. Four GPT-6-Astra judgments per submission are combined by 3-of-4 node majority; the expert check covers 41 follow-up judgments.
evidence.limitations: Only 15 computational directions, generally one attempt per agent/task, and automated judges rather than exhaustive expert review. Strict all-node grading is demanding; passing necessary conditions would not establish publication quality. The text retains stale 105-submission references and inconsistent ancillary statistics, so only Table 2/Section 4's cross-checked 135-submission results are used. Historical commit dates do not prove first public visibility; no experiments were reproduced.

entries.update_note: 2026-10-15: the primary paper documents the expanded nine-agent/135-submission evaluation, evidence-linked strict grading and expert meta-validation. October 13 project revision 3d3496430ea1 expands the earlier October 6 artifact from 342 judgments to 540 (four per submission), within this run's discovery lookback; the current README dates its release October 15. The benchmark idea predates today, and commit timestamps do not establish exact historical public visibility. Earlier artifact: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/prometheus-eval/into-the-unknown/8f531eeacd7a/README.md; expanded artifact: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/prometheus-eval/into-the-unknown/3d3496430ea1/README.md.

entries.title: Finish RL Training Faster: Bitwise-Consistent, High-Performance, Agent-Driven
summary: This engineering report makes training recomputation and vLLM rollout share a numerical execution path, aligning low-precision kernels, routing and reduction order so sampled-token probabilities match bit for bit in the tested recipes.

It documents DeepSeek and Mamba-hybrid transfers plus an agent-assisted debugging workflow, providing a practical recipe for reducing train-rollout mismatch while making the remaining throughput and training-quality trade-offs explicit.

evidence.rationale: Delayed discovery: blog front matter documents Oct 14 09:00 UTC, one hour before this daily window but within 72 h. Complete blog/technical tables and linked preview PR descriptions inspected. DeepSeek-V4-Flash GRPO uses 32 GB200 GPUs, 128 prompts x 8 responses and one update/step; over 100 steps authors report exactly zero same-weight token differences and 91.3% of baseline rollout throughput. Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B NVFP4 on 8 GB200 nodes retains training reward on a 375-task filtered SWE-bench Pro training subset. The contribution covered is the detailed dated report and transfer evidence; existing DeepSeek preview PR opened Sep 2, and bitwise consistency is not a new invention here.
evidence.limitations: No end-to-end wall-clock gain was measured; training overhead was not separately isolated. The 91.3% rollout ratio includes differing response lengths and late baseline degradation; first 89 steps give 88.6%. Each baseline has one untuned recipe without TIS/MIS; collapse is not universal. Same-weight forward equality does not prove gradient correctness or account for stale/asynchronously changed policies. Recipe requires one update/step and TP=1; speculative decoding is not covered. Code links are preview/open PRs, not an asserted upstream release. No independent reproduction.

entries.title: CacheSmith: Accurate RAG Serving under Latency SLOs with Adaptive KV Reuse
summary: CacheSmith adapts how much cross-chunk attention is recomputed when reusing cached RAG context, jointly choosing request batches and a warm-up, probe and patch plan under latency budgets.

Its objective counts responses that meet both a generation-quality gate and a first-token deadline, helping serving systems allocate recomputation where it improves useful responses rather than latency alone.

evidence.rationale: Reviewed method, planner/scheduler Algorithm 1, runtime and all evaluation/ablation sections. vLLM 0.10.2 experiments use Llama 3.1-8B on one 96 GB RTX PRO 6000 and Qwen3-32B on two, EPYC 9554 and NVMe-cached chunks. Across 96 task/arrival/SLO combinations, authors exceed an oracle best-static configuration in 93 and report 2-27.5% higher quality-gated SLO attainment. Timing is inferred from CacheSmith's PRIMARY cs.AR Oct 15 batch plus official announcement schedule; Oct 13 is receipt, not asserted public release.
evidence.limitations: Quality is estimated from offline demand profiles, not guaranteed for every request; experiments use four small benchmark-derived/synthetic tasks, Poisson/Gamma arrivals and precomputed SSD chunks. Majority signal selection can hurt minority requests in mixed batches. Query-context baselines share authors' untuned reimplementation because original kernels were unavailable. Quality gates are task-specific, not general answer correctness. No verified implementation release or independent reproduction; do not relabel the paper's 27.5% as percentage points.

entries.title: Delta Tokenizer: Reference-Identical Tokenization of Session Deltas and Segment-Parallelism for Long Prompts on Multicore CPUs
summary: Delta Tokenizer extends earlier TokTier session reuse with tokenizer-aware CPU chunking and scheduling, so long fresh prompts can share cores without delaying short agent updates or changing reference token IDs.
The paper reports 59% lower median time to first token for tested 100K-token chat contexts in SGLang, showing how to remove CPU work that remains after model-side prefix caching.

evidence.rationale: Reviewed Sections 3-6, safe-splice/cut arguments, evaluation setup, exactness checks and limitations, plus TokTier README. New paper adds normalized/special-token-safe CPU segmentation, shared chunk scheduling and expanded measurements beyond July's session-repair method. SGLang 0.5.19/Qwen3-8B on EPYC 9115/RTX PRO 6000 reports chat median 145 ms to 60 ms at 100K tokens; 16-core full encoding of 4M characters is 8.2x faster than direct serial encoding. Public availability is inferred from the Oct 15 primary cs.CL batch and official 20:00 Eastern announcement schedule, not the Oct 14 receipt timestamp.
evidence.limitations: Benefits depend on long cache-friendly sessions; cold GPU prefill can dominate with all front ends within 5%. The 23x tail result includes overlength requests declined after tokenization; admitted repeated-document tests show about 7x instead. Exactness applies to admitted frozen tokenizer configurations with fallback. Incremental/fast encoders are released, but chunk pool and SGLang adapter are promised future code. Session repair itself predates this paper in TokTier. No independent reproduction.

entries.title: Scaling Laws for Multimodal Data Mixtures
summary: This work fits multimodal pretraining laws that account for directional transfer, competition for model capacity and diminishing returns from repeated vision or audio data.

Controlled mixture-of-experts experiments make the framework useful for planning how to divide a training budget among model size, unique data and modality mixtures, while requiring coefficients to be fitted for the intended setup.

evidence.rationale: The October 14 new-submission batch and official schedule imply public availability at October 14 00:00 UTC, despite the October 10 submission date. Sections 2–6 and Appendices G–I cover 268 fitting experiments and three held-out runs; eight of nine held-out modality-loss predictions are within 2.6% of observed values.
evidence.limitations: Coefficients depend on tokenizers, discrete next-token objectives, data quality and sparse architecture. The non-text-heavy continuation underpredicts text loss by 6.73%; larger-scale and video validation remain future work. Loss prediction is not a downstream-capability guarantee, and no code release or independent reproduction was verified.

entries.title: Two Clocks: Why Larger Rollout Batches Learn Slower but Fail on Schedule in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
summary: Two Clocks separates the samples needed for learning progress from those consumed before training collapse when rollout batches and learning rates are scaled together.

Its controlled GRPO experiments motivate starting below a critical batch size and increasing the batch later, helping practitioners evaluate sample efficiency and stability separately from hardware throughput.

evidence.rationale: Availability is inferred from the October 14 primary-category new-submission batch and official schedule. Sections 3–6 and Appendices B, F and G test 512–8,192-response batches, clipping and batch ramps on Qwen math models; larger batches lose sample efficiency above a learning-rate-dependent critical scale.
evidence.limitations: The local quadratic progress model and drift-threshold failure hypothesis are conditional approximations. Most runs use a modified 1.5B math recipe with KL, entropy bonuses and gradient clipping disabled; robustness settings have limited seeds. The author-linked code repository returned 404, and no end-to-end throughput gain was established.

entries.title: Pack Light, CarryOn: Building Object-Oriented Context for Long-Horizon Agents
summary: CarryOn organizes an agent's context around versioned reusable task objects, explicit unfinished obligations and a recent interaction tail, folding history only after evidence and consistency checks.

This lets long-running agents continue from work already present in files or application state; matched Claude Opus 4.7 experiments improve OSWorld 2.0 partial score by 5.8 points while reducing total tokens by 51.9%, including context-management calls.

evidence.rationale: The detailed paper is in the October 14 batch, whose 00:00 UTC availability is inferred from the dated listing and official announcement schedule. October 13 repository preview history contains earlier headline results, although commit times do not prove first public visibility. Sections 3–4 and Appendices A–C add candidate/evidence binding, atomic folds, 40-task ablations and explicit resource accounting. Matched OSWorld 2.0 partial score rises 43.9% to 49.7%, binary success 15.7% to 19.4%; 100 BrowseComp-Plus questions rise 49% to 56%.
evidence.limitations: Only one principal host model, one 100-question browsing subset and small 40-task ablations; no independent reproduction. Grounder checks establish scoped consistency and availability, not semantic task correctness. Some comparator scores are previously reported, not matched reruns. The linked repository is a preview and explicitly postpones implementation release until after review; no available code is claimed.

entries.update_note: 2026-10-14: the detailed primary paper supplies the context-update mechanism, atomic validation and commitment protocol, complete resource accounting and controlled ablations beyond the October 13 project preview history at https://github.com/Ethannju/carryon; that history does not establish its exact first public visibility. New-paper availability at 00:00 UTC is inferred from https://arxiv.org/list/cs.AI/recent?skip=0&show=2000 and https://info.arxiv.org/help/availability.html. The idea and preview headline are not claimed to have first appeared today.

entries.title: Using specialized data to improve research agent accuracy
summary: Parallel compares the same research agent with public-web access alone and with additional PubMed and ClinicalTrials.gov connectors on 288 LABBench2 questions.

Structured specialist access yields 12 net additional correct answers and illustrates how constrained search, complete records and web-to-database handoffs can improve evidence retrieval even when similar data is publicly indexed.

evidence.rationale: The dated October 13 primary report specifies matched agent/model/processor configurations, 168 LitQA3 and 120 TrialQA questions, unchanged benchmark scoring and inspected call traces. Errors change 34 to 22 overall; 15 questions improve and three regress. Connector calls complement web searches for literature questions and often substitute for general lookups on trial records.
evidence.limitations: Vendor-authored study with one run per question per condition, no reported confidence interval or repeated-seed analysis, and no isolated attribution across search-space and representation changes. Only two biomedical benchmark subtasks were tested; extrapolation to private legal/financial databases is speculative. Fixed per-question pricing is not a measurement of underlying compute. No paper or released experiment code was verified.

entries.title: ReTerm: Recovery Training for Self-Improving Terminal Agents
summary: ReTerm teaches terminal agents to recover from their own failed environment states, first using teacher-generated repair demonstrations and then mixing ordinary and recovery rollouts during reinforcement learning.
Its bounded queue of recent failure states keeps recovery practice aligned with the evolving policy; the authors' matched 9B-model evaluation improves Terminal-Bench 2.0 from 20.2% to 34.8% Pass@1.

evidence.rationale: October 14 batch; arXiv submission October 13 at 14:44:24 UTC. Sections 3–4 describe pre-verifier VM snapshots, teacher-only SFT loss and separate group normalization for original/recovery tasks. Table 4 reports 25.8% for recovery SFT, 28.0% for standard GRPO and 34.8% for ReTerm-GRPO. Three alternative harnesses retain 6.7–12.4-point gains; accessible implementation history begins with October 14 05:52:49 UTC initial release.
evidence.limitations: The principal study uses Qwen3.5-9B trained on 16 A100-80GB GPUs, verifier-based synthetic terminal tasks and a fixed evaluation seed. Most other model comparisons come from original papers/releases and are not matched reruns. Recovery analysis uses model judging with manual verification; except tool-use errors, recovery rates remain at or below 32%. No independent experiments were reproduced.

entries.title: Prorsa: Unleashing the Potential of Prefill-Decode Disaggregation in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Prorsa monitors agent trajectories, sandbox startup and tool execution to forecast short-term prefill and decode demand, then switches rollout workers between the two roles.

This adapts disaggregated inference to multi-turn reinforcement learning, reducing interference and cache-capacity bottlenecks; the authors report 1.11–4.05x faster agentic rollouts, with slowdowns in most tested single-turn math settings.

evidence.rationale: Sections 3–5 inspect workload characterization, lifecycle prediction and adaptive allocation atop Verl/SGLang. Experiments use FP8 Qwen3-235B-A22B, DeepSeek-V3.2 and MiMo-V2.5-Pro on a 16-server, 128-GPU cluster with NVLink and 400-Gbps RDMA NICs, comparing rollout time against prefill-decode colocation. Role switching adds 1.0–1.44x over task-tuned static splits in the MiMo ablation. The October 12 v1 submission predates its verified October 14 announcement batch.
evidence.limitations: Rollout speedups do not measure full training time or final policy quality. Results depend strongly on attention parallelism and task mix; KV transfer and switching can hurt single-turn workloads. Decode allocation forecasts admission-cache volume without explicitly predicting output lengths or near-term cache reclamation. GPU model and a dedicated code release were not verified.

entries.title: FastEEP: Fast Intra-Instance Elastic Scaling for Expert-Parallel MoE Serving
summary: FastEEP resizes expert-parallel MoE serving instances by reusing worker processes, communication structure and address-stable runtime state while changing which GPUs actively participate.

This lets a running service release or reacquire individual GPUs with shorter reconstruction delays; the authors report 4.5–11.7x faster resizing than their vLLM Elastic EP baseline on supported comparisons.

evidence.rationale: Sections 3–6 describe persistent-parent NCCL subgroups, NIXL peer masks, CUDA virtual-memory offload and coordinated worker transitions. Six MoE models are evaluated on two eight-H20-3e nodes with NVLink and 400-Gbps RDMA; resizing takes 4.2–13.4 seconds, while the compared vLLM Elastic EP takes 36.4–92.0 seconds. ShareGPT experiments also measure service interruption, distinct from overall scaling latency.
evidence.limitations: This is a 16-GPU evaluation, not demonstrated hundred-rank scaling. Expansion remains bounded by the initialized maximum topology and available memory; dormant state consumes host memory. Resizing still interrupts token output. The Elastic EP baseline cannot run two of the six models, so its speedup range excludes those comparisons. A specific open-source repository or PR was not verified.

entries.title: Extending Inductor for the IBM Spyre Accelerator
summary: IBM explains how its Spyre backend extends PyTorch Inductor with graph-wide tensor layouts, explicit scratchpad planning and compile-time work distribution for a dataflow accelerator.

The engineering report offers concrete guidance for adapting a shared compiler to unfamiliar hardware, with measured kernel improvements and a smaller custom backend rather than a claimed end-to-end LLM speedup.

evidence.rationale: The October 13 report adds compiler-design and evaluation detail beyond the October 8 native-device integration already covered. Publication metadata is 05:45:30 PDT, after the October 13 cutoff.
